Siza's tidal swimming pools at Leça da Palmeira, set into the rocks by the sea, are a famous early work from 1966. Students and visitors now come to Porto just to see these buildings.
Daily life

x: The Metro is mostly light rail and runs across the top deck of the Dom Luís I Bridge
The francesinha, a sandwich of meats under melted cheese and a beer-and-tomato sauce, is the local comfort food
Like Lisbon, Porto faces rising rents as tourist flats spread through the historic centre

deep.w: Livraria Lello inspired Hogwarts in Harry Potter
deep.r: J.K. Rowling, who lived in Porto in the early 1990s, has said she never visited the bookshop

deep.x: Porto has joined its granite old town and bold new buildings into one confident identity.

cards.text:
O Porto reinventou-se desde os anos 2000, com arquitetura emblemática, um Metro ligeiro, um turismo em grande crescimento e universidades cheias de vida.

É também a capital portuguesa da arquitetura: Álvaro Siza e Eduardo Souto de Moura, ambos vencedores do Prémio Pritzker, vêm da Escola do Porto.

quiz.q: Quem projetou a Ponte Luís I?
quiz.explain: Antigo sócio de Eiffel; a empresa de Eiffel construiu a Maria Pia.

quiz.q: Como é que o vinho do Porto mantém a doçura?
options: A aguardente vínica trava a fermentação
quiz.explain: As leveduras param antes de consumir todo o açúcar.

quiz.q: Para que serviam os barcos rabelos?
options: Transportar vinho do Porto pelo Douro abaixo
quiz.explain: As pipas de vinho iam das quintas para Gaia.

quiz.q: Porque é que o Porto tem a alcunha de "Invicta"?
quiz.explain: As forças liberais resistiram ao exército de D. Miguel.

lessons.title: Açores e Madeira
lessons.summary: Ilhas vulcânicas no Atlântico: como se formaram, quem as povoou e como se vive lá hoje.

cards.title: Nascidas do fundo do oceano

deep.x: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the sea floor is pulling apart by roughly 2 cm a year, and molten rock wells up to fill the gap. Near the Azores this happens across an unusually broad zone, the Azores plateau, probably because a plume of hot mantle also rises beneath it. The extra melt built a cluster of volcanoes tall enough to break the surface.
Hotspot islands

Madeira formed differently. It sits over a hotspot, a long-lived column of hot mantle, while the African plate creeps slowly over it. Each volcano is carried away from the source and goes quiet, and a new one grows above the hotspot. That is why Porto Santo, to the north-east, is much older and more worn down than Madeira.
Youngest and oldest

x: **Santa Maria**, the oldest Azorean island, is the only one with marine fossils and pale sandy beaches
**Pico**, the youngest, is a near-perfect cone reaching 2,351 m, the highest point in Portugal
Porto Santo's long golden beach is made of crushed shells and old reef, not volcanic rock

deep.x: Because the islands are so young, their soils are thin on the newest lava and rich on older ash, and their coasts are mostly steep cliffs.

deep.w: The Azores are the peaks of sunken Atlantis
deep.r: They are young volcanoes built up from the sea floor; Atlantis is a legend told by Plato

deep.x: Island Portugal was made by fire from below: the Azores by plates pulling apart, Madeira by a hotspot.

cards.text:
Os dois arquipélagos são os cumes de enormes vulcões que se erguem milhares de metros acima do fundo do Atlântico.

Os Açores ficam onde se encontram três placas tectónicas, perto da Dorsal Médio-Atlântica. A Madeira fica no meio da placa africana, sobre um ponto quente de rocha do manto, quente e ascendente.

cards.title: Vulcões ainda despertos

deep.x: Since the Portuguese arrived, the Azores have seen many eruptions, on land and offshore, and hundreds of felt earthquakes. Madeira, by contrast, has had no eruption in historical times.
Capelinhos

In September 1957 a volcano began erupting from the sea just off the western tip of Faial. For about 13 months it threw out ash, steam and lava, building a new peninsula of about 2.4 km² and burying nearby villages and the lighthouse in ash. No one died, but farms and homes were ruined.

In 1958 the US Congress passed the Azorean Refugee Act, backed by Senator John F. Kennedy, which offered special visas to families hit by the eruption and opened the way for a large wave of emigration.
Earthquakes and landslides

In 1522 an earthquake set off a landslide that buried Vila Franca do Campo, then the main town of São Miguel, killing thousands. On 1 January 1980 an earthquake of about magnitude 7 struck Terceira, São Jorge and Graciosa, killing about 60 people and badly damaging Angra do Heroísmo, which was rebuilt and listed by UNESCO in 1983.
Living with it
The Capelinhos visitor centre is built underground, inside the ash, beside the half-buried old lighthouse.
The Azores' volcanoes give them fertile soils and clean energy, and occasionally take lives and homes.

cards.text:
Os Açores continuam geologicamente ativos. Os sismos são frequentes, e vários vulcões entraram em erupção desde o povoamento, tanto em terra como no mar.

A erupção dos Capelinhos, no Faial, em 1957–58, acrescentou terra nova à ilha e levou milhares de ilhéus a emigrar para os Estados Unidos.

cards.title: Ilhas desertas

deep.x: Madeira was explored by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira around 1419–20, sent by Prince Henry. Its name means "wood", after the dense forest. Settlers arrived from about 1425, and the islands were split into captaincies, each run by a captain on behalf of the crown.
Bartolomeu Perestrelo's daughter Filipa later married Christopher Columbus, who lived for a time on Porto Santo and in Madeira.
Clearing the land

Chroniclers tell that settlers set fire to Madeira's forest and it burned for seven years. That is surely exaggerated, but huge areas were cleared. Rabbits released on Porto Santo multiplied so fast that they ruined early crops. In the Azores, sheep, goats and pigs were often left on islands before settlers arrived, so there would be food waiting.
Who came

Most settlers came from the Algarve, Alentejo and Minho. On Faial and Pico, Flemish families arrived under Josse van Huerter, whose name is said to survive in the town of Horta. Enslaved Africans were also brought, especially to Madeira's sugar plantations.
Lake sediments studied in 2021 hinted that people may have visited the Azores centuries before the Portuguese, perhaps Norse sailors, but the idea is still debated.
The islands were empty when found, so their people, crops and even animals all came with 15th-century settlement.

cards.text:
Ao contrário das Canárias, a Madeira e os Açores não tinham população nativa quando os navegadores portugueses lá chegaram, no início do século XV.

Os povoadores vieram do continente e, em algumas ilhas açorianas, da Flandres. Desbravaram a floresta, trouxeram animais e culturas e construíram novas sociedades do zero.

cards.title: Açúcar, laranjas e chá

deep.x: Madeira's white gold

Sugar cane thrived on Madeira's warm south side. By around 1500 Madeira was the leading sugar producer of the Atlantic world, worked largely by enslaved people from Africa and the Canaries, and its mills and water channels became a model later copied in São Tomé and Brazil. Brazil's larger, cheaper sugar soon undercut it, and Madeira turned to wine.
The Azores' crops

Early settlers grew wheat for Portugal's forts in North Africa and woad (pastel), a plant whose blue dye sold well in Flanders. Angra, on Terceira, became a vital stop for fleets returning from India and Brazil. In the 1800s São Miguel shipped huge numbers of oranges, mostly to Britain, until disease and competition ended the trade from the 1860s.
Growers then tried new crops. Pineapples were raised in glasshouses, and tea was planted with the help of experts brought from Macau in 1878.
Today

x: Cows are said to outnumber people in the Azores, and cheeses like São Jorge are famous
Madeira grows bananas on terraces, mostly sold to mainland Portugal
Tourism is now the biggest earner in Madeira and growing fast in the Azores

deep.x: Azorean pineapple plants are "smoked" inside glasshouses with burning green plant matter, a traditional trick that makes them flower at the same time.
The islands survived by switching crops whenever markets changed, from sugar and dye to oranges, milk and visitors.

cards.text:
As economias das ilhas mudaram vezes sem conta. A Madeira teve um boom do açúcar no final do século XV e depois virou-se para o vinho. Os Açores cultivaram trigo e plantas tintureiras e depois exportaram laranjas para a Grã-Bretanha.

Hoje a pecuária leiteira domina nos Açores, enquanto na Madeira lidera o turismo.

cards.title: Um clima atlântico

deep.x: The sea changes temperature slowly, so islands far from land rarely get very hot or very cold. In Funchal, winter afternoons are often around 19–20 °C and summer days rarely pass 30 °C. Frost happens only on the highest peaks, where snow falls now and then in winter.
The Azores High

The Azores lie near a zone of high pressure over the subtropical Atlantic, the Azores High. In summer it usually grows and shelters the islands, giving long settled spells. In winter it often shifts south, and Atlantic depressions sweep through with rain and gales. The Azores therefore get much less sunshine than Madeira, and hydrangeas thrive in the damp.
Storms and floods

x: In October 2019 Hurricane Lorenzo passed close to Flores and Corvo and wrecked much of the port at Lajes das Flores
In February 2010 flash floods and mudslides in Madeira killed more than 40 people, mostly around Funchal
On steep islands, heavy rain turns into a torrent within minutes

deep.x: Madeira now builds channels and barriers in its ravines to slow these floods.
The Azores are not tropical: the sea around them is usually about 16 °C in late winter and around 23 °C at the end of summer.
The ocean is the islands' thermostat: mild all year, but open to storms from every side.

cards.text:
O oceano mantém os dois arquipélagos amenos todo o ano. A Madeira é subtropical, com invernos quentes na soalheira costa sul. Os Açores são mais frescos, húmidos e ventosos, com céus instáveis.

As montanhas criam grandes contrastes: encostas norte húmidas e nubladas e costas sul mais secas.

cards.title: Sobreviventes da laurissilva

deep.x: Laurisilva is a humid evergreen forest found in Macaronesia, the island groups of the Azores, Madeira and the Canaries. Each archipelago has its own endemic species, because plants and animals that arrived from the mainland evolved in isolation for millions of years.
The Azores' lost forest

When settlers arrived, laurel and juniper forest covered much of the Azores. Today native forest survives mainly on steep slopes, high ridges and in protected areas. Much of the land is pasture, or plantations of Japanese cedar (cryptomeria), a fast-growing timber tree introduced in the 1800s.
Invaders

x: Kahili ginger (conteira), a showy Himalayan plant, smothers the forest floor and stream banks
Australian cheesewood (incenso) has spread across lowland woods
Rangers and volunteers clear invaders and replant native species

deep.x: The priolo

The Azores bullfinch, or priolo, lives only in the native forest around Pico da Vara in eastern São Miguel. In the 1990s just a few hundred birds were thought to survive, making it one of Europe's rarest birds. Removing invaders and replanting the native plants whose seeds and buds it eats helped numbers rise to around a thousand, and its threat status has been lowered.

deep.w: Laurel forest is just a wood of bay trees
deep.r: It is a whole ecosystem of several laurel-family trees with heathers, hollies, ferns, mosses and lichens

deep.x: Laurisilva is a living relic, and on most islands it survives only where people have chosen to protect it.

cards.text:
A laurissilva da Madeira é uma sobrevivente famosa, mas esta floresta também já cobriu grande parte dos Açores. Lá, a maior parte foi cortada para campos e pastagens, e as plantas invasoras ameaçam hoje o que resta.

Proteger estas florestas protege também aves raras das ilhas, como o priolo de São Miguel.

cards.title: Da baleação à observação de baleias

deep.x: Whaling came to the Azores with American ships from New England, which stopped in the islands for water, food and crew. Many young Azoreans signed on, and some settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts. In the 1800s islanders started their own shore-based whaling.
How it worked

Lookouts in stone huts on the cliffs, the vigias, scanned the sea. When they saw a spout, they fired a rocket, and men ran from fields and homes to the boats. The canoas were light, about 11 m long, and rowed or sailed by a crew of seven. The harpooner struck by hand, and a wounded whale could drag the boat for hours. Oil was then extracted at shore factories.
The end of the hunt
Sea giants today

x: Sperm whales live around the islands all year
Blue, fin and sei whales pass through in spring on migration
Common, bottlenose and Risso's dolphins are seen on most trips

deep.x: The whalers' museum at Lajes do Pico keeps the boats, tools and stories of the hunt.
In Moby-Dick (1851), Herman Melville noted that many whaling crews were filled out with hardy Azorean islanders.
The Azores turned a hunting tradition into a watching one, using the same lookouts and knowledge of the sea.

cards.text:
Durante cerca de um século, os homens açorianos caçaram cachalotes em pequenos botes abertos, com arpões lançados à mão. O último foi morto em 1987.

Dois anos depois, a primeira empresa de observação de baleias arrancou no Pico. Hoje a observação de cetáceos é uma parte importante do turismo das ilhas.

cards.title: Como funciona a autonomia

deep.x: Autonomy was a response to geography and history. The islands are far from Lisbon, and after the 1974 revolution independence movements briefly appeared in both, notably the FLA in the Azores and FLAMA in Madeira. The 1976 Constitution answered with self-government inside the Portuguese state.
Money and taxes

The regions keep most of the taxes raised on the islands and also receive transfers from the state budget. They may lower some taxes, which is why VAT rates are lower than on the mainland. Madeira also has a low-tax International Business Centre, whose rules have been examined by the European Commission.
Outermost regions
The EU recognises nine outermost regions: the Azores, Madeira, the Canary Islands and six French territories. EU treaties allow special measures for them, such as support for transport and farming.
Politics
Madeira was led for 37 years, from 1978 to 2015, by Alberto João Jardim of the PSD. The Azores were governed by the PS from 1996 to 2020, and since then by a PSD-led coalition.
Lajes air base on Terceira, used by Allied forces since 1943, is still shared by the Portuguese and US air forces.
Autonomy lets the islands govern most daily matters themselves while remaining fully part of Portugal and the EU.

cards.text:
Desde 1976, os Açores e a Madeira são regiões autónomas, com parlamentos e governos próprios, eleitos, que tratam da maior parte dos assuntos locais.

São também "regiões ultraperiféricas" da União Europeia, o que permite apoios e regras especiais devido à distância e às pequenas economias insulares.

cards.title: Vinho da Madeira

deep.x: In the 1600s and 1700s, ships bound for India and the Americas called at Funchal and took casks of wine aboard. Merchants noticed that wine which had crossed the tropics and come back, called vinho da roda ("round-trip wine"), tasted better. Producers then found ways to copy the effect at home.
How it is made

Like port, Madeira is fortified with grape spirit, added early for sweet styles and late for dry ones. Then comes the warming. Because the wine has already been heated and exposed to air, an opened bottle keeps for months, and some bottles from the 1700s and 1800s are still drinkable.

x: **Sercial**: the driest, sharp and fresh
**Verdelho**: medium-dry
**Boal** (Bual): medium-rich
**Malvasia** (Malmsey): the richest and sweetest
**Tinta Negra**, a red grape, is the workhorse of most everyday blends

deep.x: Famous fans

Madeira was a favourite wine in colonial America, and it is often said that it was used to toast the US Declaration of Independence in 1776. Shakespeare mentions Malmsey, and an old story says the Duke of Clarence was drowned in a barrel of it in 1478.

deep.w: Madeira is just a cooking wine
deep.r: Cheap cooking Madeira exists, but the best are among the longest-lived fine wines in the world

deep.x: Madeira is the wine that thrives on the heat and air that ruin other wines.

cards.text:
O vinho da Madeira é fortificado como o do Porto, mas depois é aquecido de propósito durante meses ou anos. Esta "cozedura" dá-lhe sabores a frutos secos e caramelo e torna-o quase indestrutível.

Quatro castas clássicas dão quatro estilos, do Sercial seco à rica e doce Malvasia, a que os ingleses chamam Malmsey.

cards.title: Ilhas de emigrantes

deep.x: Small islands with large families and little land could not support everyone. Waves of emigration followed hardship: eruptions, earthquakes, crop failures and lack of work. Most Portuguese Americans, about 1.4 million people, have Azorean roots. Money sent home by emigrants paid for houses, churches and festas across the islands.
Communities abroad

In the US, cities such as Fall River and New Bedford in Massachusetts, and farming towns in California's Central Valley, have large Azorean communities with their own Holy Spirit festas. Madeirans built a big community in Venezuela; since that country's economic crisis in the 2010s, many have returned to Madeira.
New arrivals

x: Low-cost flights to Ponta Delgada began after air links were opened up in 2015, and Azores tourism grew fast
Madeira's airport, named after Cristiano Ronaldo in 2017, has a runway extended over the sea on tall concrete pillars
Remote workers have settled in places like Ponta do Sol, Madeira, which opened a "Digital Nomad Village" in 2021

deep.x: Funchal's New Year fireworks were recognised by Guinness World Records in 2006 as the largest fireworks display in the world.
The islands' story is one of leaving and returning: emigrants carried their culture abroad, and now the world comes to them.

cards.text:
Durante séculos, viver nas ilhas significou emigrar. Os açorianos foram para o Brasil, depois para a Nova Inglaterra, a Califórnia e o Canadá. Os madeirenses foram para a Venezuela, a África do Sul, o Brasil e o Reino Unido.

As comunidades emigrantes mantêm laços fortes com a terra, enquanto o turismo, os voos mais baratos e o teletrabalho trazem agora gente nova às ilhas.

quiz.q: O que formou a Madeira?
options: Um ponto quente sob a placa africana
Um pedaço de África que se separou
quiz.explain: A placa desliza lentamente sobre uma coluna quente do manto.

quiz.q: Que erupção de 1957–58 levou à emigração para os EUA?
quiz.explain: Os EUA aprovaram o Azorean Refugee Act em 1958.

quiz.q: Quando foi caçado o último cachalote nos Açores?
quiz.explain: A observação de baleias começou dois anos depois.

quiz.q: O que torna o vinho da Madeira único?
quiz.explain: Por estufagem ou em canteiro.

lessons.title: A língua portuguesa
lessons.summary: Do latim da Galécia a uma língua global com cerca de 260 milhões de falantes.

cards.title: Do latim ao português

deep.x: The Romans landed in Iberia in 218 BC, during their war with Carthage, and needed about two centuries to conquer the west. The Lusitanians, led by Viriathus, resisted fiercely until he was murdered in 139 BC. Soldiers, traders and settlers brought not the polished Latin of Cicero but the everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin.
Regular sound changes
Portuguese is easy to recognise by a few changes that happened again and again:

x: An l between vowels disappeared: dolorem became dor, salire became sair
An n between vowels vanished, often leaving a nasal vowel: luna became lua, manum became mão
Pl-, cl- and fl- at the start of a word turned into ch-: plenum became cheio, flamma became chama
The group -ct- became -it-: noctem became noite, lactem became leite
Latin pluvia
pl- becomes ch-
Portuguese chuva (rain)

deep.x: Germanic traces

After Rome fell, the Germanic Suebi and then the Visigoths ruled the north-west. They soon adopted Latin but left a few dozen words, many of them military, such as guerra (war), guardar (to guard) and roubar (to rob), plus the colour branco (white).

deep.w: Portuguese is a kind of "broken Spanish"
deep.r: Portuguese and Spanish are sister languages that grew separately from spoken Latin

deep.x: Portuguese is Latin that kept changing, in regular steps, for two thousand years.

cards.text:
O português é uma língua românica: nasceu do latim do dia a dia falado no ocidente romano da Península Ibérica.

Ao longo de muitos séculos, esse latim foi mudando som a som até se tornar uma língua nova. A maioria das palavras portuguesas ainda vem do latim, mesmo quando hoje parecem muito diferentes.

cards.title: O galego-português

deep.x: The language took shape between the 9th and 12th centuries in the old Kingdom of Galicia, which reached south to the Douro. Formal documents were still written in Latin, but scribes let local words slip in, and by around 1200 whole texts appeared in the spoken language. Besides Afonso II's will, an early example is the Notícia de Torto, a list of grievances from the same years.
Why they split

x: Portugal's centre moved south to Coimbra and then Lisbon, where the language mixed with the Romance speech of the reconquered south
Galicia was ruled from Castile, so Castilian became the language of power and writing there
Portuguese gained its own court, chancery, university and, later, printing presses

deep.x: Close cousins today

Galician is co-official with Spanish in Galicia, a region of about 2.7 million people. A farmer from the Minho and one from Ourense can usually chat with little effort, and many Galicians watch Portuguese television. Spelling hides some of the closeness: Galician writes ñ and ll where Portuguese writes nh and lh.
Some Galicians, known as reintegrationists, argue that Galician should use Portuguese spelling, and a few associations already write it that way.
Portuguese and Galician began as one language; borders and politics, not distance, pulled them apart.

cards.text:
Na Idade Média, as pessoas das duas margens do Minho falavam uma só língua, hoje chamada galego-português.

Quando Portugal se tornou um reino independente e se expandiu para sul, a sua fala afastou-se da da Galiza, que ficou sob Castela. O galego e o português continuam a ser parentes muito próximos.

cards.title: Palavras vindas do árabe

deep.x: The Moors held Lisbon until 1147 and the Algarve until 1249. Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side, and many Christians under Muslim rule spoke a Romance dialect full of Arabic terms. As the Portuguese kingdom moved south, it took over farms, irrigation channels, markets and workshops, together with the words for them.
The telltale al-
Arabic al means "the". Portuguese usually borrowed nouns with the article attached, which is why so many Arabic loans start with al- or a-.
Names on the map

x: Alcântara: al-qantara, "the bridge"
Albufeira: al-buhayra, "the lagoon"
Alcácer do Sal: al-qasr, "the castle"
Fátima: an Arabic woman's name, borne by the Prophet's daughter

deep.x: Most of these names cluster south of the Tagus, where Muslim rule lasted longest. In the Minho and Trás-os-Montes they are much rarer.
Oxalá, "let's hope so", probably comes from the Arabic phrase "law sha' Allah", "if God wills"; Spanish has the same word, ojalá.

deep.w: Arabic left only a handful of words
deep.r: Estimates run to several hundred everyday words, and many more counting place names

deep.x: Arabic gave Portuguese a whole layer of everyday words, many still recognisable by the al- at the start.

cards.text:
A partir de 711, grande parte da Península Ibérica foi governada por estados muçulmanos; no que é hoje o sul de Portugal, até 1249.

O árabe era a língua do saber, da agricultura e do comércio, e o português absorveu várias centenas das suas palavras, da cozinha às obras, além de topónimos por todo o sul.

cards.title: Os trovadores

items: Cantigas de amigo: voz de uma moça
Cantigas de amor: lamento de um homem

deep.x: The fashion began with the troubadours of southern France, whose songs travelled along the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela. Poets in north-west Iberia adapted it, and Galician-Portuguese became so prestigious that Castilians wrote poetry in it too. Alfonso X of Castile composed over 400 songs to the Virgin Mary, the Cantigas de Santa Maria, in Galician-Portuguese, even though he wrote his laws in Castilian.
Three kinds of song

items.b: a girl longs for her love
a man pines for a lady

deep.x: The cantigas de amigo are the most original. Though written by men, they speak in a young woman's voice, often by the sea, at a spring or under a hazel tree, waiting for her "amigo". Their refrains and repeated lines suggest roots in older folk songs.
A poet king
King Dinis, who reigned from 1279 to 1325, left about 137 cantigas, more than almost any poet of his time; Alfonso X was his grandfather.

x: Martin Codax, a jogral from Vigo, left seven songs about the sea, six of them with their music, a rare survival
The songs reach us through three main songbooks: the Cancioneiro da Ajuda in Lisbon and two later Italian copies, now in the Vatican Library and Portugal's National Library

deep.x: The insult songs can be startlingly crude: poets mocked cowardly knights, stingy patrons and each other in terms that still make readers blush.
For about 150 years, Galician-Portuguese was the language Iberian poets used to sing about love.

cards.text:
Nos séculos XIII e XIV, o galego-português era a língua da moda da poesia lírica em toda a Ibéria cristã.

Reis, nobres e jograis errantes compunham cantigas de amor, de saudade e de troça. Sobrevivem cerca de 1700 destas cantigas, copiadas num punhado de cancioneiros medievais.

cards.title: Camões e Os Lusíadas

deep.x: Camões was born around 1524, probably in Lisbon, and lived a restless life. He lost an eye fighting in North Africa, was jailed after a street brawl in Lisbon, and sailed for India in 1553. He spent about 17 years in the East, in Goa and possibly Macau, before returning home poor.
The poem

The epic follows Gama's fleet from Lisbon to Calicut while the gods of Olympus argue over the sailors: Venus protects them and Bacchus plots against them. On the way, characters tell Portuguese history, from Viriathus to Aljubarrota. It opens with "As armas e os barões assinalados", "arms and the famous heroes", an echo of Virgil's Aeneid.
The poem is not pure praise. As the fleet leaves Belém, the Old Man of Restelo condemns the greed and vanity that drive the empire.
Fixing the language

Portuguese grammar was being written down at the same time: Fernão de Oliveira published the first grammar in 1536 and João de Barros another in 1540. Camões's vocabulary and style then served as a model for writers for centuries.
According to tradition, Camões survived a shipwreck at the mouth of the Mekong by swimming ashore with his manuscript held above the water.
Camões turned a sea voyage into the founding poem of the Portuguese language.

cards.text:
Luís Vaz de Camões deu ao português a sua grande epopeia. Os Lusíadas, impressos em 1572, recontam a viagem de Vasco da Gama à Índia como a história de todo um povo.

O seu êxito ajudou a fixar o português como língua literária, que ainda hoje é muitas vezes chamada "a língua de Camões".

cards.title: Além dos oceanos

items: Língua do comércio nos portos asiáticos
Crioulos em África e na Ásia

deep.x: Portuguese spread in two different ways. In Brazil, and later in Angola and Mozambique, it became the language of settlers, the state, the Church and schools. In much of Asia it spread as a contact language: merchants, interpreters and local traders used a simplified Portuguese with each other, even when no Portuguese were present. Dutch and English traders arriving in the 1600s often had to learn it to do business.
Creoles
Where people of many origins mixed, new languages formed, with mostly Portuguese words but a grammar of their own.
Papiamento, spoken in Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire, also has a strong Portuguese element, though linguists debate how it began.
Words that travelled

x: Swahili meza (table), from mesa
Hindi and Bengali chabi (key), from chave, and Konkani and Marathi pav (bread roll), from pão
Japanese kappa (raincoat), from capa
English marmalade, from marmelada, quince paste, and cobra, from cobra de capelo

deep.w: Creoles are just broken Portuguese
deep.r: They are full languages with their own grammar; Kriolu alone is the mother tongue of about a million people

deep.x: Portuguese travelled first as a tool of trade, and it left words and whole new languages wherever ships called.

cards.text:
A partir do século XV, navegadores, mercadores e missionários portugueses levaram a língua pelas costas de África, da Ásia e da América do Sul.

Durante cerca de dois séculos, serviu de língua franca comercial em muitos portos. Deixou para trás novas línguas crioulas e um rasto de palavras emprestadas.

cards.title: Cerca de 260 milhões de falantes

deep.x: Counting speakers is never exact. Censuses ask different questions, and in Africa many people speak Portuguese as a second or third language alongside local ones. The figure of about 260 million, used by the Instituto Camões among others, includes both native speakers and fluent second-language speakers.
Where they live

x: Portugal, ~10.5 million speakers
÷ ~260 million in total
≈ 4% of all speakers

deep.x: Growing in Africa

Angola and Mozambique have young, fast-growing populations, and Portuguese is spreading as the language of cities, schools and media. In Luanda many children now grow up with Portuguese as their first language. Demographers expect Africa's share of speakers to keep rising through this century.
Where it counts

Portuguese is also one of the most used languages online, usually ranked in the top ten for websites and social media, largely thanks to Brazil. It is not one of the six official languages of the United Nations, a status Portuguese-speaking countries have long asked for.
São Paulo state alone has about 45 million people, more than four times the population of Portugal.
Portugal is the birthplace of Portuguese, but its future is being written mostly in Brazil and Africa.

cards.text:
O português tem cerca de 260 milhões de falantes, o que o coloca entre as dez línguas mais faladas do planeta.

Cerca de oito em cada dez vivem no Brasil. Portugal tem apenas uns 4% dos falantes do mundo, e a fatia de África é a que cresce mais depressa.

cards.title: Europeu e brasileiro

deep.x: Sounds

Brazilians pronounce unstressed vowels clearly, while the Portuguese swallow many of them. In much of Brazil, t and d before an i sound become "tch" and "dj", so dia sounds like "djia". In Portugal, and in Rio de Janeiro, an s at the end of a syllable sounds like "sh".
Grammar

x: Ongoing actions: Portugal says "estou a ler", Brazil "estou lendo", for "I'm reading"
Pronoun position: Portugal says "chamo-me", Brazil usually "me chamo"
"You": in Portugal tu is for family and friends and você can sound distant; in most of Brazil você is the normal word, though tu survives in the south and parts of the north-east

deep.x: False friends

items.b: PT has a cold, BR constipated

deep.x: In writing, Angola, Mozambique and the other African countries generally follow the European standard, though each has its own accent, slang and local words.
Brazilian telenovelas, starting with Gabriela in 1977, made Brazilian accents and expressions familiar to a whole generation in Portugal.
Two standards, one language: the differences are real, but smaller than they first sound.

cards.text:
O português europeu e o brasileiro são uma só língua com duas normas, um pouco como o inglês britânico e o americano.

Diferem na pronúncia, em alguma gramática, no vocabulário e na forma corrente de dizer "tu/você". Os falantes entendem-se bem, com uma ou outra gargalhada por causa dos falsos amigos.

cards.title: O Acordo Ortográfico de 1990

deep.x: Separate reforms in 1911 in Portugal, after the Republic, and in 1943 in Brazil put the two countries on different paths. A common agreement in 1945 failed because Brazil never applied it, and Portugal kept its own rules until the new agreement took effect.
What changed in Portugal

x: Silent consonants dropped: acção became ação, óptimo became ótimo, director became diretor
Months and seasons lost their capitals: Janeiro became janeiro
K, W and Y officially joined the alphabet, making 26 letters
Some hyphens went: hei-de became hei de

deep.x: What changed in Brazil

Brazil dropped the diaeresis, so lingüiça became linguiça, and some accents, so idéia became ideia and vôo became voo. By commonly cited estimates, the agreement changed about 1.5% of words in Portugal and about 0.5% in Brazil.

x: Consonant pronounced in Portugal, silent in Brazil
Portugal keeps facto, Brazil writes fato
Both spellings are correct

deep.x: Still unfinished

Angola has not ratified the agreement, and its use across Africa and in Timor-Leste is uneven. In Portugal, some writers, newspapers and citizens' groups still reject it, while supporters argue that a common spelling helps schools, dictionaries and international use.

deep.w: The agreement made Portuguese and Brazilian spelling identical
deep.r: Many differences remain, because spelling still follows each country's pronunciation

deep.x: The 1990 agreement brought the two spellings much closer, but not into one.

cards.text:
Durante a maior parte do século XX, Portugal e o Brasil escreviam muitas palavras de forma diferente.

O Acordo Ortográfico, assinado em Lisboa em 1990, fixou regras comuns para todos os países de língua portuguesa. Demorou décadas a aplicar e ainda é debatido, mas as escolas e os textos oficiais em Portugal e no Brasil já o seguem.

cards.title: Sons que baralham quem aprende

deep.x: Nasal vowels

Portuguese has five nasal vowels, made by letting air flow through the nose as well as the mouth, plus nasal diphthongs such as ão, õe and ãe. They are marked by a tilde or by an m or n closing the syllable. The difference changes meaning, so a learner who drops the nasal can say something quite different.
Vanishing vowels

In European Portuguese, unstressed vowels shrink or disappear. An unstressed e often vanishes completely, so telefone sounds close to "t'lefon'". An unstressed o turns into a u sound, so porto ends in "u". Strings of consonants result, which is why the language can sound clipped to outsiders.
Tricky letters

x: lh and nh sound like Italian gli and gn, as in filho and vinho
Initial r and rr are a throaty sound for most speakers, but some older people in the north and interior still roll them
In the Minho and much of the north, v and b often merge, so vinho can sound like "binho"
X can sound like "sh" (xadrez), "z" (exame), "ks" (táxi) or "s" (próximo)

deep.x: In parts of the Minho and Trás-os-Montes, some speakers still say ch as "tch", the way all Portuguese did in the Middle Ages, so chave sounds like "tchave".
European Portuguese is spoken far more compactly than it is written, and learning to hear the missing vowels is half the battle.

cards.text:
O português europeu soa mais suave e compacto do que a escrita sugere; há estrangeiros que até o confundem com uma língua eslava.

Quem aprende tem dificuldade com as vogais nasais, as vogais átonas que quase desaparecem e o s final que soa a "ch". Só a letra x tem quatro sons diferentes.

quiz.q: Que palavra latina deu origem a "chave"?
quiz.explain: O cl- latino em início de palavra passou a ch-.

quiz.q: Que língua deu ao português aldeia, açúcar e almofada?
quiz.explain: Séculos de domínio muçulmano deixaram centenas de palavras árabes, muitas começadas por al- ou a-.

quiz.q: Em que língua escreviam as suas cantigas de amor os poetas medievais de toda a Península Ibérica?
quiz.explain: Até Afonso X de Castela escreveu nela as suas Cantigas de Santa Maria.

quiz.q: Em que se costuma tornar o "estou a ler" de Portugal no Brasil?
quiz.explain: O Brasil usa o gerúndio para ações em curso.

quiz.q: O que mudou o acordo de 1990 na ortografia de Portugal?
options: Eliminou muitas consoantes mudas, como em ação
Tornou toda a grafia igual à do Brasil
quiz.explain: Acção passou a ação e óptimo passou a ótimo.

lessons.title: O mundo lusófono
lessons.summary: A CPLP, nove países, antigos entrepostos na Ásia e a diáspora portuguesa.

cards.title: A CPLP

deep.x: The CPLP was founded on 17 July 1996 by seven countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, and São Tomé and Príncipe. Its headquarters are in Lisbon, and its leaders meet at a summit every two years, with a rotating presidency.
What it does

x: Runs the International Institute of the Portuguese Language, based in Praia, Cape Verde
Coordinates cooperation on health, education, justice and election observation
Since a 2021 agreement signed in Luanda, eases visas and residence between members

deep.x: The newest member

Equatorial Guinea was a Spanish colony, but its islands of Bioko and Annobón were Portuguese until a 1778 treaty handed them to Spain, and Annobón still speaks a Portuguese-based creole. The country added Portuguese as an official language in 2010 and joined in 2014. One condition, abolishing the death penalty, was met with a 2022 law.
Strengths and limits

Members differ hugely in size, wealth and political system, and decisions need consensus. Critics see the CPLP as more a forum than a powerful organisation; supporters point to its role in Timor-Leste's independence and in crises in Guinea-Bissau. Dozens of countries, from Japan to Uruguay, have joined as associate observers.
Portugal used the 2021 mobility agreement to create a special CPLP residence permit, and tens of thousands of people from member countries applied within months.
The CPLP turns a shared language into a club of nine countries, loose but lasting.

cards.text:
A Comunidade dos Países de Língua Portuguesa, a CPLP, foi fundada em Lisboa em 1996. Tem hoje nove membros em quatro continentes, onde vivem cerca de 300 milhões de pessoas.

Promove a língua, a cooperação e a circulação entre os membros, mas não tem mercado comum nem exército.

cards.title: Brasil

deep.x: For three centuries Brazil's wealth came from sugar, then from gold and diamonds in Minas Gerais in the 1700s, and later from coffee. Much of it was built on the labour of enslaved Africans: around 4 to 5 million were taken to Brazil, more than to any other country in the Americas. Brazil abolished slavery only in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so.
The court in Rio

When Napoleon's army invaded Portugal in 1807, the royal family and much of the court sailed to Rio de Janeiro, which became the capital of the empire. In 1815 Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal to Portugal. After King João VI returned to Lisbon in 1821, his son Pedro stayed and declared independence on 7 September 1822, becoming Emperor Pedro I. He later returned to Portugal and, as Pedro IV, fought a civil war to win the throne for his daughter.
Ties today

x: Brazilians in Portugal number several hundred thousand, by far the largest foreign community
Millions of Brazilians have Portuguese ancestry, and many hold Portuguese passports
Brazilian music, from bossa nova to sertanejo, is part of everyday life in Portugal

deep.x: Rio de Janeiro is often described as the only city outside Europe ever to serve as the capital of a European empire, from 1808 to 1821.
Brazil began as Portugal's colony and grew into its giant sibling, with twenty times its population.

cards.text:
O Brasil é, de longe, o maior país lusófono, com cerca de 213 milhões de habitantes.

Colónia portuguesa desde 1500, tornou-se independente em 1822 com um príncipe português. Hoje os laços vão nos dois sentidos: os brasileiros são agora a maior comunidade estrangeira em Portugal.

cards.title: Angola

deep.x: The navigator Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo river in 1482, and Luanda was founded in 1576. For centuries the colony was above all a source of enslaved people shipped to Brazil. Large-scale Portuguese settlement came only in the 20th century, and by 1974 a few hundred thousand settlers lived there.
Languages

Angola has many national languages, among them Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo. Since independence, Portuguese has spread as the language of schools, cities and national unity. In the 2014 census about 70% of people said they spoke it, and in Luanda it is the home language of most families.
Oil and the economy

Oil makes up around nine-tenths of Angola's exports, so the economy rises and falls with world oil prices; diamonds come second. Angola left OPEC, the oil exporters' club, in 2024. Portuguese banks, builders and retailers are active there, and Angolan investors own stakes in Portuguese companies.
Culture
Angolan music crossed to Lisbon: kizomba and the fast electronic kuduro fill dance floors there, and slang such as "bué", meaning "loads", entered everyday Portuguese.
During Portugal's crisis in the early 2010s, Angola became a leading destination for Portuguese emigrants, reversing the flow of 1975.
Angola is a young, oil-rich country where Portuguese is turning from an official language into a mother tongue.

cards.text:
Angola, na costa sudoeste de África, é o segundo maior país lusófono em população, com cerca de 37 milhões de habitantes.

Rica em petróleo e diamantes, reconstruiu-se desde o fim de uma longa guerra civil, em 2002. O português está a espalhar-se depressa e é hoje a língua materna de muitos jovens angolanos.

cards.title: Moçambique

deep.x: Vasco da Gama called at Mozambique Island in 1498 on his way to India. The island, long the colonial capital, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 1898 the capital moved south to Lourenço Marques, renamed Maputo after independence.
Many languages

Emakhuwa is the most widely spoken first language, followed by languages such as Xichangana and Cisena. Portuguese works as the common language of government, schools and towns, and is the main language of most people in Maputo.
Neighbours and the Commonwealth

Surrounded mostly by English-speaking countries, Mozambique joined the Commonwealth in 1995. English is widely learnt for trade with South Africa, where generations of Mozambicans have worked in the mines.
Mozambicans and Portugal
Mozambique's flag is the only national flag that shows a modern rifle, crossed with a hoe and resting on a book.
Mozambique uses Portuguese as a common thread between dozens of languages, while looking to its English-speaking neighbours.

cards.text:
Moçambique estende-se ao longo da costa sudeste de África, no Índico, com cerca de 34 milhões de habitantes.

O português é a língua oficial e uma ponte entre dezenas de línguas locais, embora só uma minoria o fale em casa. Foi também o primeiro membro da Commonwealth que nunca tinha sido colónia britânica.

cards.title: Cabo Verde

deep.x: Portuguese navigators reached the islands around 1456–1462 and settled Santiago soon after. Ribeira Grande, now Cidade Velha, became the first European colonial town in the tropics and a major hub of the Atlantic slave trade. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.
Kriolu and morna

Kriolu grew from Portuguese and West African languages, and each island has its own variety. Morna, the slow, melancholy song made famous worldwide by Cesária Évora, the "barefoot diva" from São Vicente, was recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage in 2019. Faster styles include funaná and coladeira.
A nation of emigrants

Droughts and famines, especially in the 1940s, drove many to leave. Large communities live around Boston in the United States, in Portugal, the Netherlands, France and Luxembourg. Money sent home is a big part of the economy, alongside tourism on beach islands such as Sal and Boa Vista.

x: Since multiparty elections began in 1991, governments have changed peacefully at the ballot box
The islands are dry: rain is scarce and much drinking water comes from desalination

deep.x: The name "Cape Verde", "green cape", refers to a headland near Dakar in Senegal, not to the islands, which are mostly dry and brown.
Ten dry islands, a creole language and a worldwide diaspora make Cape Verde a small country with a long reach.

cards.text:
Cabo Verde é um arquipélago de dez ilhas vulcânicas a cerca de 600 km da costa ocidental africana. Estava desabitado quando os portugueses lá chegaram, por volta de 1460, e tornou-se uma encruzilhada do Atlântico.

Em casa fala-se crioulo e na escola português, e há mais cabo-verdianos a viver no estrangeiro do que nas ilhas.

cards.title: Guiné-Bissau e São Tomé

deep.x: Guinea-Bissau

Portuguese traders worked this coast from the 1440s, but control inland stayed weak for centuries. In 1956 Amílcar Cabral, an agronomist born in Bafatá, co-founded the PAIGC, which fought for the independence of both Guinea and Cape Verde. Cabral was assassinated in January 1973; the country declared independence that September, and Portugal recognised it in 1974.

Since independence the country has seen repeated coups and political crises. Most people farm, and cashew nuts are by far the main export. The Bijagós islands, where hippos swim in salt water, are a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
São Tomé and Príncipe

The islands were empty when the Portuguese arrived around 1470. Plantations of sugar, then cocoa and coffee, relied on enslaved and later contract workers from the mainland. In 1909 British chocolate makers led by Cadbury boycotted the islands' cocoa over conditions close to slavery.

x: The equator crosses Ilhéu das Rolas, an islet just south of São Tomé
With about 230,000 people, it is one of Africa's smallest countries
Forro and other creoles are spoken alongside Portuguese, which most people use

deep.x: In February 1953 colonial authorities killed hundreds of local people in the Batepá massacre; 3 February is now a national holiday in São Tomé.
Two small countries, one on the mainland and one at sea, both shaped by plantations, liberation and creole languages.

cards.text:
A Guiné-Bissau, no continente africano ocidental, conquistou a independência depois de uma luta armada liderada pelo movimento de Amílcar Cabral.

São Tomé e Príncipe, duas pequenas ilhas no golfo da Guiné, já esteve entre os maiores produtores de cacau do mundo. Nos dois países, um crioulo de base portuguesa é a língua do dia a dia para muita gente.

cards.title: Timor-Leste

deep.x: The Portuguese arrived in the early 1500s, drawn by sandalwood. The island was later split with the Dutch, whose western half became part of Indonesia. As Portugal withdrew in 1975, the Fretilin movement declared independence, and Indonesia invaded nine days later and annexed the territory.
Occupation and resistance

Violence, famine and disease under the occupation cost an estimated 100,000 to 180,000 lives. The 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili, filmed by a foreign journalist, drew world attention, and Bishop Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996.
Portugal's cause

When the referendum of August 1999 was followed by militia violence, huge crowds in Portugal dressed in white, formed human chains and stopped for minutes of silence to demand international action. A UN-mandated force arrived that September.
Languages

Tetum is the main everyday language. Portuguese was chosen as co-official partly as a symbol of the resistance, which had used it. Indonesian and English are widely understood, and more than a dozen local languages are spoken.
The name means "East East": timur is Malay for east, and leste is Portuguese for east.
Timor-Leste kept Portuguese as a sign of its fight for independence, and Portugal backed that fight loudly.

cards.text:
Timor-Leste, a metade oriental da ilha de Timor, foi português durante cerca de quatro séculos.

Depois de 24 anos de ocupação indonésia, o seu povo votou pela independência em 1999, e tornou-se um Estado em 2002. O português e o tétum são as suas línguas oficiais.

cards.title: Macau e Goa

deep.x: Macau

Portuguese traders settled Macau around 1557 with the consent of Chinese officials. For centuries it linked China, Japan and Europe and served as a base for missionaries. Under a 1987 agreement it was handed to China on 20 December 1999 as a Special Administrative Region, keeping its own laws and economy for 50 years, until 2049.

x: Portuguese is official alongside Chinese, though only a small fraction of residents speak it
The Historic Centre, with Senado Square's wavy calçada, has been a UNESCO site since 2005
Since 2003 China has used Macau as the venue of a trade forum with Portuguese-speaking countries

deep.x: Goa

Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa in 1510 and it became the capital of Portuguese Asia. In December 1961 Indian troops entered Goa, Daman and Diu, ending Portuguese rule; Portugal recognised this only after 1974. Konkani is the official language, and about a quarter of Goans are Catholic. Many Goans born before 1961, and their descendants, can register as Portuguese citizens.
Macau's famous egg tarts were popularised in 1989 by an English baker, Andrew Stow, who adapted the Lisbon pastel de nata.
Macau and Goa no longer speak much Portuguese, but they still eat, build and name things in a Portuguese way.

cards.text:
Macau, na costa sul da China, foi português durante mais de 400 anos, até 1999, e Goa, na Índia, durante mais de 450 anos, até 1961.

Hoje pouca gente lá fala português, mas o legado continua vivo nas igrejas, nos nomes das ruas, na comida, nos apelidos e no direito.

cards.title: A diáspora na Europa

deep.x: The great wave of the 1960s and 1970s built communities in France, Germany and Luxembourg. A second wave came after 2000, and especially during the crisis years of 2011–2014, when over 100,000 people a year left. Many were young graduates, and the UK became a leading destination until Brexit.
France

Counting children and grandchildren, France's Portuguese community is usually estimated at well over a million people. Portuguese surnames are common in French football, politics and business, and Portuguese is taught in some French state schools.
Switzerland and Luxembourg

In Switzerland, the Portuguese are one of the largest foreign communities, working in construction, hotels, cleaning and care. In Luxembourg they are the largest foreign nationality, and Portuguese is heard everywhere from building sites to bank offices.
Keeping in touch

x: Portuguese abroad elect four of the 230 MPs: two for Europe and two for the rest of the world
Community associations, Portuguese schools and RTP Internacional keep the language alive
Summer festivals in home villages fill up with returning families

deep.w: Emigration is a thing of the past
deep.r: Tens of thousands of Portuguese still leave each year, while Portugal now also receives many immigrants

deep.x: Portugal is a small country with a large second population spread across Europe.

cards.text:
Cerca de dois milhões de pessoas nascidas em Portugal vivem no estrangeiro, uma das proporções mais altas de qualquer país europeu.

A maioria está na Europa, sobretudo em França, na Suíça, no Reino Unido e no Luxemburgo. Os seus filhos, os lusodescendentes, mantêm muitas vezes a língua e laços fortes com as aldeias dos pais.

cards.title: A diáspora nas Américas

deep.x: Islanders had strong reasons to leave: tiny farms, earthquakes and eruptions, and few jobs. From the 1800s, Azorean men signed on to American whaling ships calling at Horta and Flores, and many settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, then the whaling capital of the world.
United States

Massachusetts and Rhode Island hold the largest communities, around Fall River, New Bedford and Providence. The Ironbound district of Newark, New Jersey, is famous for its Portuguese restaurants and bakeries. In California's Central Valley, Azorean families built a large part of the dairy industry.
Canada and Venezuela

Organised emigration to Canada began in 1953, when the ship Saturnia landed Portuguese workers at Halifax. Toronto's Little Portugal and Montreal's Plateau grew from that wave. In Venezuela, tens of thousands of Madeirans ran shops, bakeries and supermarkets; since Venezuela's crisis of the 2010s, many have returned to Madeira.

x: Bermuda, Hawaii and South Africa also have long-established Portuguese communities
Azorean festivals of the Holy Spirit are celebrated from Massachusetts to California

deep.x: After the Capelinhos volcano erupted on Faial in 1957–58, a special US law let thousands of Azoreans emigrate to America.
From whaling ships to dairy farms, islanders from the Azores and Madeira carried Portugal deep into the Americas.

cards.text:
Do outro lado do Atlântico, cresceram comunidades portuguesas no Brasil, nos Estados Unidos, no Canadá e na Venezuela, muitas vindas dos Açores e da Madeira.

Cerca de 1,3 milhões de americanos e uns 450 000 canadianos declaram ascendência portuguesa, das vilas piscatórias da Nova Inglaterra a Toronto.

quiz.q: Onde fica a sede da CPLP?
quiz.explain: A Comunidade foi fundada em Lisboa em 1996.

quiz.q: Que país aderiu à CPLP em 2014, depois de tornar o português língua oficial?
quiz.explain: Uma antiga colónia espanhola com passado português em Ano Bom.

quiz.q: Que país lusófono é membro da Commonwealth?
quiz.explain: Aderiu em 1995.

quiz.q: Quais são as duas línguas oficiais de Timor-Leste?
quiz.explain: O tétum é a principal língua do dia a dia.

quiz.q: Em que estado dos EUA ficam as comunidades portuguesas de Fall River e New Bedford?
quiz.explain: Baleeiros açorianos fixaram-se lá no século XIX.

lessons.title: Portugal no século XX
lessons.summary: Ditadura, guerras coloniais, revolução e Europa.

cards.title: A vida no Estado Novo
cards.text: O regime de Salazar assentava em "Deus, Pátria, Família". Censurava a imprensa, proibia partidos e greves, usava a polícia política PIDE e mantinha Portugal pobre e sobretudo rural, com muita emigração.

deep.x: António de Oliveira Salazar, an economics professor, became finance minister in 1928 and prime minister in 1932. His 1933 constitution created the **Estado Novo** ("New State"), which lasted until 1974, one of Europe's longest dictatorships.
How control worked

x: Censors with the famous "blue pencil" cut newspapers, books, films and songs
The PIDE political police used informers, torture and the Tarrafal prison camp in Cape Verde
Elections were held, but the opposition was harassed and the results managed
Strikes were illegal; workers and bosses were organised in state "corporations"

deep.x: A poor country

Salazar balanced the budget and kept Portugal out of the Second World War, but he distrusted industry and mass education. Most people lived from small farms; many homes had no electricity or running water.
Women's lives were tightly limited: a married woman needed her husband's permission for some jobs and to travel abroad, and nurses and air hostesses long faced marriage restrictions.
The Estado Novo bought stability with silence: no free press, no free parties and very little change.
Opponents later summed up the regime's popular culture as the "three Fs": Fado, Fátima and Futebol.

cards.title: Emigração
cards.text: Dos anos 1950 aos anos 1970, bem mais de um milhão de portugueses emigraram, muitos ilegalmente ("a salto"), para França, Alemanha e Luxemburgo, fugindo da pobreza e do serviço militar.

deep.x: Portugal had always sent people abroad, mostly to Brazil. After about 1960 the flow turned to Europe, where France and West Germany were booming and short of workers. Between 1960 and 1974 roughly 1.5 million Portuguese left, out of a population of under 9 million.
Leaving "a salto"

The state limited legal emigration, so many people went clandestinely. They paid smugglers ("passadores") to guide them on foot over the mountains into Spain and across the Pyrenees into France. Young men also fled to avoid being sent to fight in Africa.
Life abroad

Many first lived in shanty towns, such as the bidonville at Champigny-sur-Marne near Paris, and worked in construction, factories and cleaning. They sent money home, and built houses in their villages that you can still spot today.
Emigration was the Portuguese people's own way out of poverty and war when the regime offered neither.
Every August, emigrants returning home on holiday became so visible that the month's festivals in northern villages still revolve around "os emigrantes".

cards.title: As guerras coloniais
cards.text: A partir de 1961, Portugal combateu os movimentos de independência em Angola, na Guiné-Bissau e em Moçambique. Ao longo de 13 anos, cerca de 800 000 portugueses serviram nas forças armadas; morreram cerca de 9000, e muitos mais africanos.

deep.x: While Britain and France were giving up their African colonies, Salazar insisted that Angola, Mozambique and Guinea were "overseas provinces" of one nation "from Minho to Timor". Independence movements, blocked from peaceful change, took up arms.
Three fronts

Guinea was the hardest front: by the early 1970s the PAIGC controlled much of the countryside. Fighting was mostly guerrilla war: ambushes, mines and raids, with napalm and forced resettlement of villagers on the Portuguese side. Massacres such as Wiriyamu in Mozambique (1972) were exposed abroad.
The cost

Conscripts served up to four years. Tens of thousands came back wounded or with lasting trauma, long rarely discussed. African deaths, among fighters and civilians, were far higher, though exact numbers are uncertain.
The colonial wars drained Portugal's money and young men, and the soldiers who fought them ended up overthrowing the regime.

deep.w: The wars were far away and barely touched daily life
deep.r: Almost every family had a son, brother or husband in Africa

cards.title: Humberto Delgado
cards.text: Nas eleições presidenciais de 1958, o general Humberto Delgado desafiou o regime. Questionado sobre o que faria a Salazar, respondeu: "Obviamente, demito-o!" Perdeu numa votação fraudulenta e foi assassinado pela PIDE em 1965.

deep.x: Humberto Delgado was an air force general who had served the regime loyally. He had lived in the USA and Canada and came back convinced that Portugal needed democracy. In 1958 he stood for president against the regime's candidate, Admiral Américo Tomás.
"Obviously, I'll sack him"

At a press conference in Lisbon's Café Chave d'Ouro on 10 May 1958, a journalist asked what he would do with Salazar if elected. His answer, "Obviamente, demito-o!", electrified the country. Huge crowds greeted him in Porto and Lisbon, and police charged the crowds.
Fraud and exile

The official result gave Delgado about a quarter of the vote. Most historians think the real result was much closer, but there was no free count. Afterwards the regime ended direct presidential elections. Delgado sought asylum in the Brazilian embassy and went into exile.
The murder

In February 1965 PIDE agents lured him to the Spanish border near Badajoz, pretending to be opposition contacts. They killed him and his Brazilian secretary, Arajaryr Campos. Their bodies were found weeks later.
One sentence from a general showed that the regime's support was far thinner than it claimed.
Lisbon's airport has been officially named Aeroporto Humberto Delgado since 2016.

cards.title: De Salazar a Caetano
cards.text: Salazar ficou incapacitado em 1968, depois de uma queda, e foi substituído por Marcelo Caetano, que prometeu reformas mas manteve as guerras coloniais e o essencial do regime.

deep.x: In August 1968 Salazar, then 79, fell from a deckchair at his summer residence in Estoril and later suffered a brain haemorrhage. President Américo Tomás replaced him in September with Marcelo Caetano, a law professor and long-time regime insider.
The "Marcelist Spring"

Caetano's motto was "evolution in continuity". Censorship was eased a little, the PIDE was renamed DGS, some exiles such as Mário Soares were allowed back for a time, and the economy grew. A "liberal wing" of young deputies, including Francisco Sá Carneiro, entered parliament hoping to reform from inside.
Spring turns to winter

x: The wars went on and costs kept rising
The liberal deputies resigned in frustration by 1973
The 1973 oil shock hit prices hard
In February 1974 General António de Spínola published "Portugal e o Futuro", arguing the wars could not be won militarily

deep.x: Caetano changed the regime's tone but not its core, and the war he would not end brought it down.
Salazar lived until July 1970; according to many accounts those around him never told him he was no longer in charge.

cards.title: 25 de Abril, 1974

events.l: "Grândola, Vila Morena" na rádio dá o sinal
Caetano rende-se no Largo do Carmo

cards.text: A 25 de Abril de 1974, jovens oficiais do Movimento das Forças Armadas (MFA) derrubaram o regime quase sem derramamento de sangue. As multidões encheram as ruas e puseram cravos nas espingardas dos soldados: a Revolução dos Cravos.

deep.x: The Armed Forces Movement (MFA) began among captains tired of endless war, frozen careers and a regime with no way out. They planned the coup in secret and used radio songs as signals.
The day

Captain Salgueiro Maia led a column from the cavalry school in Santarém to Lisbon's Terreiro do Paço, then surrounded the Carmo barracks, where Caetano had taken refuge. Despite radio appeals to stay home, crowds poured into the streets to support the soldiers. That evening Caetano handed power to General Spínola.
Carnations

A restaurant worker, Celeste Caeiro, had carnations left over from a cancelled celebration. She gave one to a soldier, who put it in his rifle barrel; others copied, and the red carnation became the symbol of the revolution.
The only deaths came when DGS agents fired on the crowd outside their Lisbon headquarters. Political prisoners were freed from Caxias and Peniche days later.
These "three Ds" summed up the MFA's programme.
A coup by soldiers became a revolution because the people joined in.
25 April is a national holiday, Dia da Liberdade, and every year people still march down Lisbon's Avenida da Liberdade with red carnations.

cards.title: A descolonização

events.l: Moçambique, Cabo Verde, São Tomé e Príncipe, Angola

cards.text: Depois da revolução, Portugal reconheceu a independência da Guiné-Bissau (1974), de Moçambique, de Cabo Verde, de São Tomé e Príncipe e de Angola (1975). Cerca de meio milhão de "retornados" chegou a Portugal.

deep.x: The MFA wanted to end the wars quickly, and the liberation movements wanted full independence, not the federation Spínola had imagined. Within about 18 months every African colony was independent.
Angola's tragedy

In Angola three rival movements fought each other as independence approached, each backed by foreign powers. The civil war that followed lasted, with pauses, until 2002. Mozambique also suffered a long civil war (1977–92).
The retornados

Hundreds of thousands of Portuguese settlers fled, many with only a suitcase. An emergency airlift in 1975 brought many home. They often arrived in a country they barely knew, sometimes facing suspicion, and were housed in hotels, camps and with relatives.
Timor and Macau
East Timor was invaded by Indonesia in December 1975; it won independence only in 2002 after a long struggle that Portugal championed. Macau was handed to China in 1999, ending the Portuguese empire.
Decolonisation was fast and chaotic, and its human costs fell on Africans and on returning Portuguese alike.
Portuguese is now an official language in nine countries, and the CPLP links them as a community.

cards.title: Construir a democracia

events.l: constituição e eleição do primeiro presidente

cards.text: Depois de um período turbulento (PREC), a constituição de 1976 instituiu uma república democrática. As eleições livres, a imprensa livre e o poder local democrático ganharam raízes.

deep.x: The 19 months after the revolution are known as the **PREC** (Processo Revolucionário em Curso). Parties of every kind appeared, banks and big industries were nationalised, and in the Alentejo farm workers occupied large estates.
Hot summer

In 1975 the country was split. Communists and parts of the military pushed for a revolutionary state, while moderate parties, the Church and much of the north resisted; party offices were burned. On 25 November 1975 moderate officers stopped a radical military uprising, and the path to parliamentary democracy was secured.
The first free votes
The election of 25 April 1975 had the highest turnout in Portugal's history. The Socialists of Mário Soares came first, ahead of the Popular Democrats; the Communists got about 12%.
Settling down
The 1982 revision abolished the military Council of the Revolution, putting the armed forces fully under civilian control. Two IMF programmes (1977 and 1983) dealt with debts left by the upheaval.
Portugal's democracy emerged from a revolution that was turbulent but, compared with many, remarkably peaceful.

deep.w: The revolution was over on 25 April 1974
deep.r: The struggle over what kind of democracy lasted until at least late 1975

cards.title: A entrada na Europa
cards.text: Portugal aderiu à Comunidade Económica Europeia a 1 de janeiro de 1986, juntamente com Espanha. Os fundos europeus ajudaram a construir estradas, escolas e hospitais; Portugal adotou o euro em 1999 (moedas e notas em 2002).

deep.x: For Mário Soares, joining the European Community was the way to anchor democracy and modernise the economy. Portugal applied in 1977. After long negotiations the treaty was signed at the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon on 12 June 1985, and Portugal joined, with Spain, on 1 January 1986.
What changed

Billions of euros in structural and cohesion funds paid for motorways, bridges, sewers, schools and training. Farmers and fishermen had to adapt to European rules and competition. Portugal grew fast in the late 1980s and 1990s.
The euro
Portugal joined the euro at its launch in 1999. When notes and coins arrived in 2002, people converted every price in their heads.
1 euro = 200.482 escudos

x: A coffee at 100 escudos

deep.x: Europe gave Portugal money, markets and a democratic anchor, and in return Portugal had to compete in a much larger game.
Portugal has held the rotating presidency of the EU Council four times; the 2007 Lisbon Treaty, signed in the Jerónimos Monastery, still sets out how the EU works.

cards.title: A Expo '98 e o Portugal moderno
cards.text: A Expo '98, em Lisboa, transformou a zona ribeirinha oriental e mostrou um país moderno. Desde então, Portugal enfrentou crises (o resgate de 2011) e tornou-se um grande destino turístico e tecnológico.

deep.x: Expo '98 ran from May to September 1998 on the theme of the oceans, marking 500 years since Vasco da Gama reached India by sea. It turned a run-down industrial area of oil depots and a slaughterhouse in eastern Lisbon into the Parque das Nações.
Crisis and recovery

After 2008, high debt and weak growth caught up with Portugal. In 2011 it needed a €78 billion bailout from the EU and IMF (the "troika"), with deep cuts, tax rises and unemployment peaking around 17% in 2013. Many young people emigrated. Portugal exited the programme in 2014.
A new image

x: Tourism boomed, especially in Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve
The Web Summit moved to Lisbon in 2016, and start-ups followed
Portugal won Euro 2016, and António Guterres became UN Secretary-General in 2017
Housing costs rose sharply, a major political issue today

deep.x: In a generation, Portugal went from a closed, poor dictatorship to an open European democracy, with booms and busts along the way.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge, with its viaducts, is about 17 km long; it was the longest in Europe when it opened in 1998.

quiz.q: O que deu, na rádio, o sinal de arranque da revolução de 25 de Abril de 1974?
quiz.explain: A canção de Zeca Afonso.

quiz.q: Quando aderiu Portugal à Comunidade Económica Europeia?
quiz.explain: Juntamente com Espanha.

quiz.q: Que general ficou famoso por dizer "Obviamente, demito-o!"?
quiz.explain: Na campanha eleitoral de 1958.

lessons.title: Como Portugal é governado
lessons.summary: A Constituição, o Presidente, o parlamento, o Governo, os tribunais, as regiões e o poder local.

cards.title: A Constituição de 1976

deep.x: The Constituent Assembly elected on 25 April 1975 spent almost a year drafting the text amid the turmoil of the revolution. The result is long and detailed, with about 300 articles, and gives a large place to social rights such as health, education, housing and work.
What it contains

x: Freedoms of expression, assembly, religion and the right to strike
A ban on the death penalty and on life imprisonment
A national health service that is universal and tends to be free, and free compulsory schooling
Principles that no revision may remove, such as the republican form of government, universal suffrage and the separation of Church and State

deep.x: How it changes

The Assembly of the Republic may revise the Constitution five years after the last revision, or at any time if four-fifths of MPs agree to open the process. Each change needs a two-thirds majority, and the President cannot veto a revision.

x: 230 MPs
two-thirds needed
at least 154 votes to change the text

deep.w: The death penalty was abolished in 1976
deep.r: Portugal abolished it for civil crimes in 1867, among the first countries; the Constitution confirmed the ban

deep.x: The 1976 Constitution is the rulebook that every law, government and court in Portugal must obey.

cards.text:
A Constituição portuguesa foi aprovada a 2 de abril de 1976 por uma assembleia eleita um ano depois da revolução.

Define Portugal como uma república democrática baseada na dignidade da pessoa humana, no Estado de direito e na separação de poderes. Já foi revista sete vezes e continua a ser a lei suprema.

cards.title: O Presidente

deep.x: Portugal's system is often called **semi-presidential**: power is shared between a directly elected President and a Government that answers to parliament. In practice the Prime Minister leads day-to-day policy, while the President's power lies in a few strong but rarely used tools and in public influence.
The veto

When the Assembly sends a law, the President has 20 days to sign it or veto it, or 8 days to ask the Constitutional Court to check it. The Assembly can override a political veto by confirming the law with an absolute majority of MPs, or two-thirds for some kinds of law. A veto of a government decree is final.

x: 230 MPs
absolute majority = more than half
116 votes override a veto

deep.x: Dissolution

The President can dissolve the Assembly and call early elections, but not in the six months after it was elected, nor in the last six months of the presidential term, nor during a state of emergency. Because it is so drastic, it is nicknamed the "atomic bomb"; it was used three times between 2021 and 2025.
Elections

Candidates must be Portuguese citizens by origin, aged at least 35, and nominated by 7,500 to 15,000 voters, not by parties. To win in the first round a candidate needs more than half of the valid votes; otherwise the top two meet in a run-off three weeks later.
Every President elected since 1976 has gone on to win a second term.
The President rarely governs but holds the keys: who becomes Prime Minister and when the people vote again.

cards.text:
O Presidente da República é o chefe de Estado, eleito diretamente pelo povo por cinco anos e limitado a dois mandatos consecutivos.

O papel é sobretudo o de árbitro. O Presidente não governa, mas nomeia o primeiro-ministro, pode vetar leis e pode dissolver o parlamento.

cards.title: A Assembleia da República

deep.x: What MPs do

x: Pass laws on almost every subject, including all laws on rights, elections and crimes
Approve the State Budget each year, usually in the autumn
Question ministers and the Prime Minister in regular debates and committees
Elect, by two-thirds, 10 of the 13 Constitutional Court judges and the Ombudsman

deep.x: Where MPs come from

The country is divided into 22 constituencies: the 18 mainland districts, the Azores, Madeira, and two for Portuguese living abroad, one for Europe and one for the rest of the world, each electing two MPs. The other seats are shared according to the number of registered voters, so Lisbon elects 48 MPs and Portalegre just 2.
Who can sit

Any voter can stand, but only on the list of a party or coalition; independents can appear on those lists. Since 2019, lists must include at least 40% of each sex. The Assembly is led by its own President, the second-highest office of the state after the President of the Republic.
The São Bento Palace was the Monastery of São Bento da Saúde until religious orders were abolished in 1834; parliament has met there ever since.
The Assembly is where the people's vote turns into laws, budgets and the rise and fall of governments.

cards.text:
A Assembleia da República é o parlamento português, uma câmara única com 230 deputados eleitos por quatro anos.

Faz leis, aprova o Orçamento, pode derrubar o Governo e elege titulares de cargos importantes. Reúne-se no Palácio de São Bento, em Lisboa, um antigo mosteiro beneditino.

cards.title: O método de Hondt
example: Maiores quocientes: A 10 000, B 8000, A 5000, B 4000, A 3333
A ganha 3 mandatos, B 2, C nenhum

deep.x: How it works

Each list's votes are divided by 1, 2, 3 and so on. The seats go, one at a time, to the largest numbers in the whole table until all are filled. In effect, each new seat goes to the list that would have the most votes per seat after winning it.
Big and small constituencies

There is no legal minimum share of the vote, but constituency size matters a lot. In Lisbon, with 48 seats, a party can win a seat with around 2% of the vote. In a district with only 2 or 3 seats it may need 20% or more. That is why smaller parties win most of their MPs in Lisbon, Porto and Setúbal.
Rough threshold for one seat ≈ 100% ÷ (seats + 1)

x: Portalegre, 2 seats
Seat 1 to A; then B's 35 beats A's 20

deep.x: Strengths and criticisms
Proposals for reform, such as a national top-up constituency or letting voters choose candidates within lists, come up regularly but have not been adopted.
Portugal also uses d'Hondt for town councils, parish assemblies and its 21 seats in the European Parliament.
d'Hondt shares seats in proportion to votes, but its rounding favours larger parties, most of all where seats are few.

cards.text:
Os mandatos são distribuídos por representação proporcional: os partidos ganham lugares mais ou menos de acordo com os votos.

Portugal usa o método de Hondt, criado pelo jurista belga Victor d'Hondt em 1878. Em cada círculo, os eleitores escolhem uma lista partidária, não candidatos individuais.

cards.title: O Governo e o primeiro-ministro

deep.x: After an election, the President meets every party that won seats and then appoints as Prime Minister the person most likely to have parliament's support, usually the leader of the largest party or coalition. The Prime Minister proposes the ministers, whom the President then appoints.
Facing parliament

Within ten days, the new Government presents its programme to the Assembly. It does not need a vote of approval: it falls only if an absolute majority of MPs, 116, votes a motion of rejection. This rule lets minority governments take office, which has happened often since 1976.
How a government ends

x: A general election and a new Assembly
The Prime Minister's resignation or death
A censure motion passed by an absolute majority, or a lost confidence vote
Dismissal by the President, allowed only to protect the regular functioning of democratic institutions

deep.x: How it works inside

The Council of Ministers, all the ministers chaired by the Prime Minister, meets weekly to approve decree-laws and bills to send to parliament. The Prime Minister's official residence is a mansion behind the parliament building in São Bento.
Single-party absolute majorities are rare: they happened only in the elections of 1987, 1991, 2005 and 2022.
In Portugal a government does not need parliament's approval to start, only to avoid a majority voting against it.

cards.text:
O Governo dirige o país no dia a dia: propõe o Orçamento, dirige a administração pública e pode aprovar decretos-leis.

É chefiado pelo primeiro-ministro, nomeado pelo Presidente tendo em conta os resultados eleitorais. Um governo só se mantém enquanto o parlamento não o rejeitar nem o censurar.

cards.title: O Tribunal Constitucional

deep.x: How judges are chosen

Ten judges are elected by the Assembly with a two-thirds majority, which in practice requires agreement between the largest parties. These ten then co-opt the remaining three. At least six must be career judges from other courts; the rest are legal experts, often law professors.
How a law reaches the Court

items: Gaps: a law that is missing

deep.x: If the Court finds a law unconstitutional before it is signed, the President must veto it. Once a rule is struck down with general binding force, it stops applying everywhere. Any ordinary court must also refuse to apply a rule it considers unconstitutional, and the case can then go to the Constitutional Court on appeal.
Between 2012 and 2014, for example, the Court struck down several budget measures, including cuts to public-sector holiday and Christmas pay, ruling that they treated groups unequally.
Other guardians

Prosecutions are led by the Public Prosecution Service, which is independent of the Government and headed by the Attorney General, appointed by the President on the Government's proposal for six years.

deep.w: The Constitutional Court hears every kind of appeal
deep.r: It decides only constitutional questions; ordinary cases end at the Supreme Court

deep.x: In Portugal no law is safe until it fits the Constitution, and 13 judges have the last word on that.

cards.text:
O Tribunal Constitucional decide se as leis respeitam a Constituição e pode anulá-las. Criado na revisão de 1982, tem 13 juízes com um único mandato de nove anos.

A seu lado, tribunais independentes, o Ministério Público, o Provedor de Justiça e o Tribunal de Contas vigiam os outros poderes.

cards.title: Açores e Madeira

deep.x: Autonomy answered old grievances: islanders had long felt neglected by Lisbon, and in 1975 small independence movements briefly appeared in both archipelagos. The Constitution gave them self-government within the Portuguese state, and their autonomy is among the principles no revision may remove.
What they control

x: Their own laws on matters such as health, education, transport, tourism, fisheries and farming
Most taxes raised in the region, with the power to lower some rates within limits
Their own flags, anthems and regional holidays

deep.x: The Representative of the Republic

The President appoints a Representative of the Republic for each region, who signs or vetoes regional laws and can send them to the Constitutional Court. The Representative also appoints the President of the Regional Government in light of the regional election results, much as the President of the Republic does with the Prime Minister.
Why not the mainland?

The Constitution also foresees administrative regions on the mainland, but in a 1998 referendum about 64% voted against creating eight of them.
