Turnout was under 50%, so the result was not binding, but no regions have been created since. Mainland planning is coordinated by five regional development commissions, the CCDRs.
The Azores spread their institutions across islands: the regional parliament sits in Horta, on Faial, while the regional government is based in Ponta Delgada, on São Miguel.
Autonomy lets the islands run most of their own affairs while remaining fully part of Portugal.

cards.text:
Os Açores e a Madeira são regiões autónomas, um estatuto criado pela Constituição de 1976 devido à distância a Lisboa e à sua identidade insular.

Cada uma tem a sua assembleia eleita e o seu governo regional, que legislam sobre muitas matérias locais. A defesa, a política externa e a justiça ficam com o Estado.

cards.title: Concelhos e freguesias

deep.x: The municipality

Each municipality has two bodies, both elected every four years. The Câmara Municipal is the executive; it is led by its president, the mayor, who is the first name on the most-voted list. The Assembleia Municipal debates and approves the budget and holds the Câmara to account; it also includes the presidents of all the parish councils.
The parish

Parishes are the level closest to citizens. They look after local paths and green spaces, issue some certificates, run markets and support schools and older people. In 2013 their number was cut from about 4,260 to about 3,090 by merging many rural parishes, and some of those mergers were reversed before the 2025 local elections.
Rules and money

x: Mayors may serve at most three consecutive terms in the same municipality
Groups of citizens can run independent lists in local elections, unlike in national ones
Councils are funded by local taxes such as the property tax (IMI), a share of state taxes and EU funds
Since 2019 many tasks in education, health and social support have been transferred from the state to the municipalities

deep.x: Corvo, in the Azores, is Portugal's smallest municipality and the only one with no parish at all.
Local power in Portugal runs from big-city mayors to parish councils that know every street by name.

cards.text:
O poder local tem dois níveis: 308 municípios, os concelhos, e abaixo deles mais de 3000 freguesias.

Cada um tem órgãos eleitos que gerem serviços locais como estradas, escolas, água, resíduos e cultura. Os presidentes de câmara e de junta são muitas vezes os políticos que as pessoas conhecem melhor.

cards.title: Eleições e voto

deep.x: Election day

Voting takes place on a Sunday, usually in schools. The day before is a "day of reflection": campaigning stops, and opinion polls cannot be published until voting ends. Ballot papers list the parties with their names and symbols, and voters mark a cross.
Who runs elections

The National Elections Commission, the CNE, watches over fairness and equal treatment of candidates, while the Ministry of Internal Administration handles the logistics. Citizens are registered automatically when they get their Citizen Card. Anyone can also ask to vote early, a week before, at a polling place of their choice.
Referendums

A national referendum must be proposed by the Assembly or the Government, checked by the Constitutional Court and called by the President. It is binding only if more than half of registered voters take part, and none of the three held so far reached that level.
After the 2007 vote, parliament chose to legislate in line with the majority anyway.

deep.w: Voting is compulsory in Portugal
deep.r: The Constitution calls voting a civic duty, but there is no fine for not voting

deep.x: Portugal's elections are frequent, free and simple: a cross on a Sunday, counted in public that same night.

cards.text:
Os cidadãos a partir dos 18 anos votam nas eleições legislativas, presidenciais, autárquicas, regionais e europeias, e em referendos ocasionais.

As eleições realizam-se ao domingo, são fiscalizadas por uma comissão independente, e os votos são contados em público em cada mesa de voto.

cards.title: Portugal na UE

deep.x: Membership means that some decisions are taken jointly in Brussels, Strasbourg and Luxembourg rather than in Lisbon alone. Trade, competition rules, farming and fisheries policy, and for euro countries interest rates, are largely set at EU level. Health, schools, pensions and most taxes remain mainly national.
How Portugal takes part

Ministers vote in the Council of the EU, where many decisions use a qualified majority. The Assembly's European Affairs Committee scrutinises EU proposals, and Portuguese judges and officials work in all the institutions.

x: 27 countries
at least 15 states (55%)
representing 65% of EU citizens = qualified majority

deep.x: Portuguese at the top
José Manuel Durão Barroso was President of the European Commission from 2004 to 2014, and António Costa has chaired the European Council since December 2024.
Language and courts

Portuguese is one of the EU's 24 official languages, so every EU law is published in it and citizens can write to the institutions in Portuguese. Portuguese courts can ask the EU Court of Justice in Luxembourg how to interpret EU law, and its answer binds them.
European Parliament elections in Portugal use a single national constituency, unlike general elections with their 22.
EU membership adds a European layer to Portuguese democracy: some laws are made jointly, and Portuguese help make them.

cards.text:
Desde 1986, Portugal é membro da União Europeia, partilhando algumas decisões com outros 26 países.

Elege 21 deputados ao Parlamento Europeu, envia ministros ao Conselho e indica um comissário. Onde os tratados dão competência à UE, o direito europeu prevalece sobre o nacional.

quiz.q: Quantos lugares tem a Assembleia da República?
quiz.explain: São eleitos 230 deputados em 22 círculos eleitorais.

quiz.q: Por quanto tempo é eleito o Presidente da República?
quiz.explain: Até dois mandatos consecutivos de cinco anos.

quiz.q: No método de Hondt, os votos de cada lista são divididos por quê?
quiz.explain: Os maiores quocientes ganham os mandatos.

quiz.q: Quem decide se uma lei respeita a Constituição?
quiz.explain: Os seus 13 juízes cumprem um único mandato de nove anos.

quiz.q: Que duas regiões têm parlamento e governo próprios?
quiz.explain: São regiões autónomas desde 1976.

lessons.title: A economia portuguesa
lessons.summary: Da entrada na CEE e do resgate ao turismo, às exportações, às renováveis, às start-ups e aos salários.

cards.title: Uma economia pequena e aberta

deep.x: What the economy is made of

Services include shops, tourism, transport, property, finance and public services. Industry is smaller than in Germany or Czechia but strong in a few clusters: cars and parts, paper and pulp, cork, textiles and shoes, food and wine, and oil refining at Sines.
Wealth per person

GDP per person is roughly €27,000 a year, about 80% of the EU average once differences in prices are taken into account. That places Portugal in the lower half of the EU, and in recent years several Central European members, such as Czechia, Slovenia and Lithuania, have moved ahead of it.

x: GDP ~€285 billion
÷ ~10.7 million people
≈ €27,000 per person a year

deep.x: Open to the world

Exports of goods and services were about 30% of GDP around 2010 and close to half by the 2020s, one of the biggest changes in the economy's history. Spain is by far the largest customer, taking around a quarter of goods exports, followed by France, Germany and the United States.

deep.w: Portugal mainly lives off farming and fishing
deep.r: Farming and fishing make up only about 2% of output; services and industry produce almost everything

deep.x: Portugal is a small, service-heavy economy that lives more and more by selling to the rest of the world.

cards.text:
A economia portuguesa produz cerca de 285 mil milhões de euros em bens e serviços por ano, menos de 2% do total da UE. Dominam os serviços, como o turismo, o comércio e as finanças.

As exportações equivalem hoje a quase metade do PIB, muito mais do que no passado, pelo que o país depende muito do que vende lá fora.

cards.title: Da CEE ao euro

deep.x: The catch-up years

Between 1986 and 2000, GDP per person rose from just over half to roughly 70% of the then EU average, measured in purchasing power. Foreign investment arrived, such as the Autoeuropa car plant at Palmela, and EU funds paid for infrastructure and training. As markets prepared for the euro, interest rates fell sharply, making borrowing cheap for families, firms and the state.
Why growth stalled

x: China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and Central European countries joined the EU in 2004, competing in the low-cost textiles, shoes and assembly work Portugal relied on
Inside the euro, Portugal could no longer devalue its currency to make its goods cheaper abroad
Cheap credit flowed into housing, roads and consumption more than into productive firms
Wages rose faster than productivity, so firms lost competitiveness

deep.x: EU money

Over four decades Portugal has received well over €100 billion in EU funds, counting farm support. Since 2021 the Recovery and Resilience Plan, known as the PRR, adds about €22 billion in grants and loans for health, housing, digital and green projects.

deep.w: The euro caused the crisis on its own
deep.r: Economists point to a mix: cheap credit, weak productivity, new global competition and the 2008 financial crash

deep.x: EU entry lifted Portugal fast, but the euro's first decade showed that cheap money alone does not make an economy productive.

cards.text:
A adesão à Comunidade Europeia, em 1986, abriu mercados e trouxe muitos fundos europeus, e Portugal cresceu depressa durante cerca de 15 anos.

Depois da chegada do euro, em 1999, o crescimento abrandou a fundo. Os anos 2000 foram uma "década perdida", em que a economia quase não cresceu enquanto as dívidas se acumulavam.

cards.title: Resgate e recuperação

deep.x: Why it happened

By early 2011 the interest rate on Portugal's ten-year bonds had climbed above 7%, after Greece and Ireland had already needed rescues. The minority government resigned in March 2011 when parliament rejected its new austerity package, and in April it requested help.

items.b: about a third of the loan

deep.x: What the programme involved

x: Cuts to public wages and pensions, and higher taxes
Privatisation of the electricity company EDP, the grid operator REN, the airports company ANA and the postal service CTT
Labour market changes, such as lower severance pay
Four public holidays suspended from 2013 to 2015, then restored in 2016

deep.x: The recovery

Exports, tourism and foreign investment led the rebound. In 2019 the state recorded its first budget surplus in the democratic era. After the dip of the Covid pandemic, surpluses returned in 2023 and 2024, and public debt fell from about 135% of GDP in 2020 to about 95% in 2024.

x: Debt ~€270 billion
GDP ~€285 billion

deep.x: Portugal repaid its IMF loans early, finishing in 2018, years ahead of schedule.
The bailout years were painful, but within a decade Portugal went from rescue case to one of the eurozone's fastest debt reducers.

cards.text:
Em 2011, sem conseguir financiar-se nos mercados a juros comportáveis, Portugal pediu um empréstimo de resgate à UE e ao FMI. Seguiram-se três anos de cortes na despesa, aumentos de impostos e reformas: o tempo da troika.

Desde então a economia recuperou: o desemprego desceu, o Estado teve excedentes orçamentais em vários anos e a dívida pública caiu para menos de 100% do PIB.

cards.title: Turismo

deep.x: Who comes

The United Kingdom has long been the biggest foreign market, especially for the Algarve and Madeira. Spain, Germany and France follow, and American visitors have grown fastest in recent years, helped by new direct flights.
Where they go

Lisbon, the Algarve and Madeira dominate, while Porto and the North have grown fast since low-cost flights expanded in the 2000s and 2010s. Lisbon's Humberto Delgado airport handled over 35 million passengers in 2024 and is close to capacity; in 2024 the government chose Alcochete, across the Tagus, for a new airport.
Benefits and strains

Short-term rentals, known as alojamento local, spread fast in Lisbon and Porto from the 2010s. They helped restore run-down buildings but added to pressure on rents, and rules on new licences have been changed several times. Lisbon charges a tourist tax of €4 per person per night.

deep.w: Tourism is all about foreigners
deep.r: Portuguese residents account for roughly three in ten nights spent in tourist lodgings

deep.x: Tourism has become a pillar of Portugal's exports and jobs, and managing its side effects is now a central policy question.

cards.text:
O turismo é uma das maiores indústrias de Portugal. Os visitantes vêm pelas praias, pelas cidades, pela comida, pelo golfe e pela história, e em 2024 os alojamentos turísticos registaram cerca de 31 milhões de hóspedes.

Os gastos dos visitantes estrangeiros, cerca de 27 mil milhões de euros por ano, fazem do turismo a maior exportação individual do país.

cards.title: O que Portugal vende

deep.x: Cars

The Volkswagen Autoeuropa plant at Palmela, opened in 1995, is one of the country's largest exporters; it builds the T-Roc, almost all for export. Stellantis builds vans in Mangualde, and hundreds of suppliers make seats, tyres, wiring and glass for car plants across Europe.
Textiles and shoes

The north, from Guimarães and Barcelos to Felgueiras and São João da Madeira, has long been the heart of textiles, clothing and footwear. Hit hard by Asian competition in the 2000s, many firms survived by moving upmarket: technical fabrics, short production runs, fast delivery to European brands and their own shoe labels. Textile and clothing exports reach around €6 billion a year, and shoes about €2 billion.
Other strengths

x: Paper and pulp from eucalyptus plantations
Refined fuels from Galp's refinery at Sines, the only one left since Matosinhos closed in 2021
Moulds and plastics from Marinha Grande and Leiria
Food such as tomato paste, olive oil and tinned fish

deep.x: Portugal has become the EU's largest bicycle maker, with many factories around Águeda.
Behind the image of sun and cork, Portugal is an industrial exporter wired into European supply chains.

cards.text:
As exportações portuguesas de bens são mais variadas do que muita gente pensa. À frente estão os automóveis e componentes, seguidos de máquinas, combustíveis refinados, plásticos, papel, têxteis e calçado.

A maior parte vai para outros países da UE, sobretudo Espanha, porque as empresas portuguesas se integram nas cadeias de abastecimento europeias.

cards.title: Cortiça: líder mundial

deep.x: An industry built on one tree

Portugal has roughly a third of the world's cork oak forests, mostly in the Alentejo and the Tagus valley, yet it processes even more cork than it grows, importing raw bark from Spain and North Africa. The industry is clustered around Santa Maria da Feira, south of Porto, where hundreds of firms turn bark into finished goods. Corticeira Amorim, founded in 1870, is the world's largest cork company.
From bark to bottle

The planks rest outdoors for months, are boiled to clean and soften them, then dried. Natural stoppers are punched from the thickest planks. Thinner cork and offcuts are ground and glued into "technical" stoppers for sparkling and everyday wines; champagne corks are agglomerated cork topped with natural discs.
Beyond the bottle

x: Floor and wall tiles that are warm, quiet and springy underfoot
Insulation boards for walls and roofs
Shoe soles, sports balls, gaskets and fashion items
Heat shields that protect rockets and spacecraft at launch

deep.x: In the 2000s, screw caps and plastic stoppers took a big share of the market. The industry answered by tackling cork taint, the musty smell that spoils some wines, and by promoting cork as natural and recyclable.
Expanded cork insulation needs no added glue: heating the granules with steam releases cork's own resin, which binds them together.
Portugal turned the bark of a tree into a high-tech export industry that uses every last scrap.

cards.text:
Portugal é o maior produtor e exportador mundial de cortiça e vende cerca de 1,2 mil milhões de euros por ano ao estrangeiro.

A maior parte transforma-se em rolhas de vinho, mas a cortiça também vai para pavimentos, isolamentos, calçado e até naves espaciais. Nada se desperdiça: as aparas são trituradas em granulado e prensadas em novos produtos.

cards.title: O vinho como exportação

deep.x: Who buys

items: France: a big buyer of port

deep.x: Portugal exports less wine by volume than Spain or Italy, but its average export price has been rising as more is sold bottled and under brand names. Shared language and emigrant communities help in markets such as Brazil, Angola and Canada.
Port: a regulated brand

Port is still among the most valuable Portuguese wines sold abroad, though sales volumes have slowly fallen since the 2000s as tastes changed. Its supply is tightly managed: each year the Douro's regulator, the IVDP, sets how much grape must may be fortified into port, and each vineyard gets a share according to a grading of its site, from A downwards.

x: Fermenting grape juice
add grape spirit (~77% alcohol)
sweet port of about 20%

deep.x: Growers and pressures

Most vineyards are small family plots, and many growers sell grapes to cooperative wineries or large firms. Costs are high on steep terraces where machines cannot work, and labour at harvest is scarce. In 2024 many Douro growers struggled to sell their grapes at a fair price as unsold wine piled up, and climate change is bringing hotter, drier summers and earlier harvests.
Wine tourism has become a business of its own: quintas in the Douro and Alentejo now earn a growing share of their income from visits, meals and rooms.
Portuguese wine's economic challenge is to earn more from every bottle rather than to make more bottles.

cards.text:
Portugal produz cerca de 7 milhões de hectolitros de vinho por ano, entre os doze maiores produtores do mundo, e exporta perto de mil milhões de euros.

O vinho do Porto continua a ser o produto mais conhecido, mas os vinhos de mesa já rendem mais no total lá fora. O objetivo do setor é vender menos vinho a granel barato e mais garrafas a preços mais altos.

cards.title: Eletricidade renovável

deep.x: Where it comes from

Dams on northern rivers, built from the 1950s on, long made hydropower the backbone of the system; in wet years it supplies over a quarter of electricity, in droughts much less. From the 2000s wind farms spread along the ridges of the interior, and since about 2019 solar power has boomed, especially in the Alentejo, after auctions set record-low prices.
Quitting coal

Portugal was the fourth EU country to stop burning coal for electricity, after Belgium, Austria and Sweden. Natural gas plants and imports from Spain now fill the gaps when rain, wind and sun fall short.
Challenges

x: Sun and wind vary, so the grid needs storage: pumped-storage dams pump water uphill when power is cheap and release it later, and large batteries are arriving
Links with Spain, and through Spain to France, are limited; the Iberian blackout of 28 April 2025, which began in the Spanish grid, cut power across mainland Portugal for most of a day
Large solar farms, wind turbines and power lines sometimes face local opposition over land and landscape

deep.x: Off Viana do Castelo, WindFloat Atlantic was one of the world's first floating offshore wind farms: three large turbines on platforms anchored in water about 100 m deep.
Rain, wind and sun now power most of Portugal's homes and factories, and the next challenge is keeping that supply steady.

cards.text:
Portugal é um dos líderes europeus em eletricidade limpa. Em 2024, as renováveis, sobretudo a hídrica, a eólica e a solar, forneceram cerca de 70% da eletricidade consumida no país.

A última central a carvão fechou em 2021, e os governos fixaram metas para ir ainda mais longe até 2030.

cards.title: Start-ups e a Web Summit

deep.x: The Web Summit

Founded in Dublin in 2009, the Web Summit moved to Lisbon in 2016, drawn by state support, the large venue at Parque das Nações and the city's appeal. A 2018 agreement with the government and the city keeps it in Lisbon until 2028 in exchange for about €11 million a year. It now draws around 70,000 people each November.
Home-grown unicorns

Most of these firms keep large engineering teams in Portugal even when their headquarters are in the United States or elsewhere. Their fortunes vary: Farfetch, founded by José Neves, ran into financial trouble and was bought by South Korea's Coupang in 2024.
Why here?

x: Engineers from strong universities such as Técnico in Lisbon, FEUP in Porto and the University of Minho, at lower salaries than in London or Berlin
Good English, a time zone close to London's, quality of life and safety
Visas and tax schemes for start-ups, tech workers and remote workers
Large international firms also run tech centres in Lisbon, Porto and Braga

deep.x: Limits

Start-ups still find less local venture capital than in bigger hubs, and rising housing costs in Lisbon and Porto worry workers. Tech remains a small part of total employment compared with tourism or industry.
Many Portuguese start-ups are founded with the US market in mind from day one, registering their company there while building the product in Portugal.
Lisbon's tech scene is real and growing, though still small next to tourism or industry.

cards.text:
Desde meados da década de 2010, Lisboa e o Porto tornaram-se bases populares para start-ups tecnológicas e trabalhadores remotos.

A Web Summit, uma das maiores conferências de tecnologia do mundo, realiza-se em Lisboa todos os novembros desde 2016. Um punhado de empresas com fundadores portugueses tornou-se "unicórnio", avaliado em mais de mil milhões de dólares.

cards.title: Salários e produtividade

deep.x: Fourteen payments

Most workers receive 14 payments a year: 12 normal months plus a holiday allowance, the subsídio de férias, usually paid before the summer, and a Christmas allowance, the subsídio de Natal. To compare with countries that pay 12 times a year, multiply by 14 and divide by 12.

x: €920 × 14 payments

deep.x: Productivity
Output per hour worked is roughly two-thirds of the EU average. According to the OECD, Portuguese workers put in more hours a year than Germans, about 1,650 against 1,350, yet produce less per hour.

v.unit: hours worked per worker a year

deep.x: Why the gap?

x: Very many small firms, which invest less in machines, technology and training
A historic education gap: in 2000 over 40% of young people left school early, while today it is under 10%, but many older workers had little schooling
Low investment per worker, especially after the 2011 crisis
A large share of jobs in labour-intensive sectors such as tourism, retail and construction

deep.x: Pay and people

Because the minimum wage has risen faster than average pay, the gap between them has narrowed. Many young graduates move abroad for higher salaries, while Portugal itself attracts immigrants, who now make up more than a tenth of residents.

deep.w: The Portuguese earn less because they work less
deep.r: They work more hours than most Europeans; the gap is in output per hour

deep.x: In the long run pay follows productivity, so Portugal's wage question is above all about skills, investment and better-paid sectors.

cards.text:
Os salários em Portugal estão entre os mais baixos da Europa Ocidental. O salário mínimo nacional subiu depressa, para 920 € por mês em 2026, pago 14 vezes por ano.

O problema de fundo é a produtividade: cada hora de trabalho produz muito menos valor do que a média da UE, o que limita quanto os salários podem subir.

quiz.q: Qual é o maior cliente das exportações portuguesas?
quiz.explain: Espanha compra cerca de um quarto das exportações de bens de Portugal.

quiz.q: Portugal é o maior produtor e exportador mundial de que material?
quiz.explain: A maior parte acaba em rolhas de vinho.

quiz.q: Quando fechou Portugal a sua última central a carvão?
quiz.explain: A central do Pego fechou em novembro de 2021.

quiz.q: Quantos salários recebe por ano a maioria dos trabalhadores portugueses?
quiz.explain: Doze meses mais os subsídios de férias e de Natal.

quiz.q: Que grande conferência de tecnologia se realiza em Lisboa desde 2016?
quiz.explain: Cerca de 70 000 pessoas participam todos os novembros.

lessons.title: Portugal e o mar
lessons.summary: Um país pequeno com um oceano imenso: peixe, ondas, ciência, energia e uma costa em mudança.

cards.title: Um país pequeno, um mar enorme

deep.x: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982), a coastal state has full sovereignty over a territorial sea of 12 nautical miles, about 22 km. Beyond it, out to 200 nautical miles, about 370 km, lies the EEZ. There the state controls fish, oil, gas, minerals and energy, but other countries' ships and planes may pass freely.
Islands make the difference
Every island generates its own 200-mile zone. The Azores and Madeira lie scattered far out in the Atlantic, so each adds an enormous area of sea.

x: Land: about 92,000 km²
Sea (EEZ): about 1,700,000 km²
Ratio: about 18 to 1

deep.x: What it means

x: The navy and air force patrol it against illegal fishing and pollution
Portugal also coordinates search and rescue over an even larger part of the Atlantic, from Lisbon and Ponta Delgada
It holds potential resources, from fish to offshore wind and seabed minerals

deep.x: Most of this sea is very deep: beyond the narrow shelf, the floor drops to 3,000–5,000 m.

deep.w: Portugal is a small country
deep.r: On land it is mid-sized for Europe; counting its sea, it is one of the largest

deep.x: Counting its sea, Portugal is not a small country at all.

cards.text:
A zona económica exclusiva (ZEE) de Portugal, o mar onde controla a pesca, a energia e os recursos do fundo marinho, abrange cerca de 1,7 milhões de km². É cerca de 18 vezes a sua área terrestre e uma das maiores da Europa.

As águas em torno dos Açores representam mais de metade.

cards.title: Reclamar o fundo do mar

deep.x: Under UNCLOS, the continental shelf means the seabed and what lies beneath it, not the water above. A state automatically has rights over it out to 200 nm. Further out, usually up to 350 nm, it must show with geological and depth data that the sea floor is a natural prolongation of its territory.
Years of mapping

A special team, the EMEPC (Task Group for the Extension of the Continental Shelf), was set up in 2005 to gather the evidence. Using research ships, sonar and a remotely operated robot called Luso, able to dive to 6,000 m, it surveyed vast areas of the sea floor.
Under review

The UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, a panel of scientists, studies claims one at a time, and each review can take many years. Portugal has added updated data since 2009. Some areas overlap with seabed claimed by Spain to the south, near the Selvagens and the Canary Islands, which would have to be settled between the two countries.

x: Seabed if claim accepted ≈ 4,000,000 km²
Land ≈ 92,000 km²
About 40 times the land area

deep.x: The extended area would include seamounts and hydrothermal vents, among the least explored places on Earth.
Portugal is seeking rights to the seabed far beyond its coast through science and law rather than force.

cards.text:
Para lá das 200 milhas náuticas, um país pode reclamar direitos sobre o fundo do mar se provar que este é um prolongamento natural do seu território. Portugal apresentou essa proposta às Nações Unidas em 2009.

Se for aceite, acrescentará cerca de 2 milhões de km² de fundo marinho, elevando o total para perto de 4 milhões de km².

cards.title: Águas frias e ricas

deep.x: In summer the Azores High to the west and low pressure over hot Iberia make north winds, the nortada, blow along the coast. Because of the Earth's rotation, moving water in the northern hemisphere is deflected to the right, so the surface layer drifts west, away from the shore. Deep water, cold and full of nutrients, wells up to take its place.
A food factory

Nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates fertilise microscopic algae, the phytoplankton. They feed tiny animals, the zooplankton, which feed sardines, mackerel and anchovies, and in turn bigger fish, dolphins, seabirds and people. Upwelling coasts cover a tiny share of the world's ocean but supply a large share of the world's fish catch.
Why the south is warmer

The Algarve's south coast faces away from the north winds and is sheltered, so upwelling there is weaker. Its beaches are often several degrees warmer than those near Lisbon or in the Minho. On the west coast, a sudden cold spell in the water usually means the nortada has been blowing hard for days.
Iberia's upwelling is the northern end of the Canary Current system, one of the four great coastal upwelling regions of the world, along with those off California, Peru and south-west Africa.
Portugal's cold summer sea is the price of its rich fishing grounds.

cards.text:
Quem nada na costa oeste de Portugal sabe que o Atlântico é frio mesmo em agosto. A razão é o afloramento costeiro: no verão, os ventos de norte afastam a água superficial da costa e sobe água fria e profunda para a substituir.

Essa água profunda está cheia de nutrientes, e é por isso que estes mares são tão ricos em peixe.

cards.title: Um povo que come peixe

deep.x: Fishing has shaped coastal towns from Caminha to Vila Real de Santo António. Most of the fleet's several thousand vessels are under 12 m long and fish close to shore with nets, lines and traps. Larger trawlers and purse-seiners work further out. Fishing is now a small share of jobs, but it keeps harbours, markets and restaurants alive along the whole coast.
The sardine crisis

Sardines are the symbol of the summer festivals, but the stock off Iberia fell sharply in the 2010s. Portugal and Spain cut catches hard, at times closing the fishery for months. The stock then recovered and catches were raised again, though scientists keep a close watch, because sardine numbers swing with ocean conditions.
From boat to plate

x: Fresh fish must first be sold at public auctions (lotas) run by the state company Docapesca
Canneries in Matosinhos, Peniche and Olhão turn sardines, mackerel and tuna into tins, a tradition from the 1800s
Portugal still imports much of the fish it eats, including almost all of its cod

deep.x: Portuguese tinned fish has become a gourmet export, sold in brightly decorated tins in specialist shops around the world.
Fish is part of Portuguese identity, and keeping it on the table means fishing only what the sea can replace.

cards.text:
Os portugueses comem mais peixe e marisco por pessoa do que qualquer outro país da UE, cerca de 57 kg por ano, mais do dobro da média europeia.

Sardinhas assadas, polvo, carapau e amêijoas são comida de todos os dias, descarregada por uma frota composta sobretudo por pequenas embarcações.

cards.title: A história do bacalhau

deep.x: Salted, dried cod keeps for months without a fridge, so it suited a seafaring Catholic country with many meatless fast days. Portuguese fishermen were working the Grand Banks off Newfoundland soon after 1500, using salt from Aveiro and the Tagus.
The White Fleet

Under the Estado Novo, a state-organised "cod campaign" from 1934 aimed to make Portugal self-sufficient. Each spring the White Fleet, white-painted sailing ships and trawlers, left for months on the Grand Banks and off Greenland. Men fished alone from small flat-bottomed boats called dories, with hand lines, often in fog and icy water, and many never came home.
The hospital ship Gil Eannes sailed with them; it is now a museum in Viana do Castelo.
Why it ended

In 1977 Canada extended its fishing limits to 200 nm, closing most of the Grand Banks to foreign fleets. Overfishing then caused the collapse of Newfoundland cod, and Canada closed that fishery in 1992. Portugal turned to imports, mainly from Norway, where cod is now often salted especially for the Portuguese market.

deep.w: Bacalhau is a Portuguese fish
deep.r: It is Atlantic cod from cold northern seas; Portugal has almost no cod of its own and imports nearly all of it

deep.x: Bacalhau is a taste of history: a fish from distant northern seas that became the heart of Portuguese cooking.

cards.text:
O bacalhau não vive em águas portuguesas, mas é o prato nacional. Durante séculos, navios portugueses foram à Terra Nova e à Gronelândia pescá-lo e salgá-lo.

Hoje a maior parte vem da Noruega e da Islândia, e continua a ser comido salgado, demolhado e cozinhado de centenas de maneiras.

cards.title: As ondas gigantes da Nazaré

steps: Ondas cruzam-se na Praia do Norte

deep.x: Normally, as waves approach a coast, the shallow continental shelf slows them and drains their energy. At Nazaré, the canyon, well over 150 km long, cuts straight through the shelf to within about a kilometre of the shore, so waves arrive with much of their power intact.
How the canyon builds waves

Waves travelling over the deep canyon keep their speed, while those crossing the shallow shelf on either side slow down and bend. The two sets meet near the beach and add together into a towering peak, and local currents can steepen them further.
Records

Big-wave surfers at Nazaré use tow-in surfing: a jet-ski pulls them onto the wave, because waves this fast are almost impossible to paddle into. A second jet-ski waits to rescue them after a fall. The best season is roughly October to March, when deep Atlantic storms send long swells.
Watching

The red lighthouse at the Fort of São Miguel Arcanjo, on the headland, is the classic viewpoint, and crowds gather there on big days. Before surfers came, Nazaré was known as a fishing town, where boats were hauled up the beach by oxen.

deep.w: Nazaré's waves are caused by earthquakes or tsunamis
deep.r: They are ordinary storm swells, focused and amplified by the shape of the seabed

deep.x: At Nazaré, the shape of the seabed turns ordinary Atlantic swells into giants.

cards.text:
A Praia do Norte, na Nazaré, tem algumas das maiores ondas surfáveis do planeta, com mais de 20 m nos melhores dias de inverno.

O segredo está debaixo de água: o Canhão da Nazaré, um desfiladeiro no fundo do mar com até cerca de 5000 m de profundidade, chega quase à praia e concentra a energia da ondulação atlântica.

cards.title: Ciência e proteção do oceano

deep.x: Ocean science in Portugal has royal roots. King Carlos I, who reigned from 1889 to 1908, was a keen oceanographer who led research cruises off the coast on his yachts, collecting deep-sea fish and studying the sea. Today institutes such as IPMA, CIIMAR in Matosinhos and Okeanos at the University of the Azores carry on the work.
Life without sunlight

In the 1990s scientists found hydrothermal vents on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge south-west of the Azores, with names like Lucky Strike, Menez Gwen and Rainbow. Seawater seeps into hot rock, heats to over 300 °C and gushes out loaded with minerals. Bacteria use these chemicals for energy, and shrimps, mussels and crabs live on the bacteria, in a food web that runs without sunlight.
Protecting the sea
In the Azores network, about half of the protected area is closed to all fishing. Lisbon co-hosted the UN Ocean Conference with Kenya in 2022.
Some vents and seamounts hold metal-rich deposits, and many scientists warn that mining them could destroy ecosystems before they are understood.
Some vent microbes and animals survive temperatures and chemicals that would kill almost any other life, and are studied for clues to how life began.
Portugal's waters hold some of the Atlantic's strangest life, and the country now protects a growing share of them.

cards.text:
O enorme mar português torna o país num lugar importante para a investigação oceânica. Fontes hidrotermais no fundo do mar perto dos Açores, canhões profundos e montes submarinos acolhem vida que não existe em mais lado nenhum.

Em 2024, os Açores criaram a maior rede de áreas marinhas protegidas do Atlântico Norte, cobrindo 30% do seu mar.

cards.title: Portos e cabos

deep.x: Sines was a small fishing town until the 1970s, when the state built a large port and industrial complex there. Its great advantage is deep water close to shore, so even the largest ships can dock. A container terminal opened in 2004, and its gas terminal, receiving liquefied gas by ship, became more important to Europe after 2022.
Transshipment

Many containers at Sines are only changing ships. Giant vessels drop boxes that smaller ships carry on to other ports in Europe, Africa and the Mediterranean. This makes Sines Portugal's busiest container port and a link in global trade routes.
The cable coast

Almost all intercontinental internet traffic travels through undersea fibre-optic cables. Portugal's position makes it a natural landing point. The EllaLink cable, opened in 2021, links Sines directly with Fortaleza in Brazil, and other cables reach Africa and the United States. Large data centres are being built at Sines to use these links.

items: Cables to Africa and the US

deep.x: Sines is the birthplace of Vasco da Gama, whose statue stands by the castle overlooking the port.

deep.w: Ships are old-fashioned in the internet age
deep.r: About 80% of world trade by volume still travels by sea, and the internet itself runs mostly on undersea cables

deep.x: Portugal's coast is a crossroads for both ships and data, linking Europe to the Atlantic world.

cards.text:
Portugal fica junto a algumas das rotas marítimas mais movimentadas do mundo, entre a Europa, a África e as Américas. O seu maior porto, Sines, é um polo de águas profundas para porta-contentores e energia.

No fundo do mar passam cabos de fibra ótica que ligam a Europa à África e às Américas, vários deles a amarrar na costa portuguesa.

cards.title: Vento e ondas ao largo

deep.x: WindFloat Atlantic has three turbines of about 8.4 MW each, 25 MW in total, about 20 km off the coast where the sea is around 100 m deep. Each stands on a triangular floating platform held in place by chains and anchors. The platforms were assembled in port and towed out to sea, avoiding costly work offshore.
Why floating

Fixed turbines on foundations work in water up to about 50–60 m deep, as across much of the North Sea. Off Portugal, such depths are often only a few kilometres from shore. Floating platforms can go into deep water, where winds are strong and steady.
Plans and doubts

The government has mapped areas for offshore wind off Viana do Castelo, Leixões, Figueira da Foz, Ericeira and Sines, and plans auctions for several gigawatts. Fishermen worry about losing fishing grounds, and floating wind still costs more than wind on land, so the timetable remains uncertain.
Wave power

The Aguçadoura wave farm near Póvoa de Varzim was the world's first multi-machine wave farm, in 2008, but it ran only briefly because of technical and financial problems. Waves remain a promising but hard-to-harvest resource.
Pico, in the Azores, had one of the world's first wave power plants connected to a grid, which worked on and off from 1999 until 2018.
Deep water close to shore turned a handicap into an opportunity: Portugal learned to float its wind turbines.

cards.text:
A plataforma continental portuguesa é estreita, por isso o fundo do mar desce a pique a partir da costa. Isso exclui, na maior parte dos sítios, as eólicas offshore fixas comuns.

Em vez disso, Portugal foi pioneiro na eólica flutuante: o parque WindFloat Atlantic, ao largo de Viana do Castelo, inaugurado em 2020, foi o primeiro do género na Europa continental.

cards.title: O nível do mar e a costa

deep.x: Sand on the west coast moves mostly from north to south, pushed by waves that usually arrive from the north-west. This longshore drift is fed by rivers, especially the Douro. Dams built in the 20th century trapped much of that sediment, and long jetties at ports such as Leixões and Aveiro block the flow further. Beaches to the south of them are starved of sand.
Sea level rising

Cascais has one of the oldest tide gauges in the world, recording since 1882. It shows sea level rising by about 20 cm since then, and the rate has increased in recent decades. Global projections for 2100 range from roughly 30 cm to about 1 m above recent levels, depending mainly on future greenhouse gas emissions.
Defend, adapt or retreat

x: **Groynes and seawalls**: rock barriers protect places like Espinho, but often push erosion further south
**Sand nourishment**: pumping sand from offshore or harbours onto beaches, as at Costa da Caparica
**Managed retreat**: removing buildings from the most exposed spots, as on some barrier islands of the Ria Formosa

deep.w: The coastline is fixed
deep.r: Coasts always move; the problem is that people have built right up to a shoreline that is now retreating

deep.x: Portugal's coast is retreating because the sea is rising and its sand supply has been cut, and living with it means giving the coast room.

cards.text:
Longos troços da costa portuguesa estão a recuar à medida que as praias e as dunas perdem areia. As barragens retêm os sedimentos que os rios antes traziam, e os molhes dos portos bloqueiam a deriva natural da areia.

O nível do mar também está a subir, por isso as tempestades chegam mais para o interior. Localidades como Espinho e a Costa da Caparica gastam muito a defender as suas praias.

quiz.q: Que tamanho tem, aproximadamente, a zona económica exclusiva de Portugal?
quiz.explain: Cerca de 18 vezes a sua área terrestre.

quiz.q: Porque é que o mar da costa oeste portuguesa é frio no verão?
quiz.explain: Os ventos de norte empurram a água superficial para o largo.

quiz.q: O que torna as ondas da Nazaré tão grandes?
quiz.explain: O canhão concentra a energia da ondulação.

quiz.q: Porque é que Portugal usa eólicas flutuantes no mar?
options: Flutuar é mais barato em todo o lado
O fundo do mar fica fundo perto da costa
quiz.explain: As fundações fixas só servem em águas pouco profundas.

lessons.title: A vida selvagem de Portugal
lessons.summary: Natureza à nossa porta.

cards.title: Um hotspot de biodiversidade
cards.text: Portugal fica no hotspot mediterrânico, com influências atlânticas e mediterrânicas, além das ilhas únicas da Madeira e dos Açores.

deep.x: A **biodiversity hotspot** is a region with an unusually high number of species found nowhere else, which has also lost much of its original habitat. The Mediterranean Basin is one of about 36 hotspots worldwide, with around 25,000 plant species, roughly half of them endemic (found only there).
Portugal sits at a crossroads. Three of Europe's biogeographical regions meet within its borders.
Two climates, one small country
Mainland Portugal has more than 3,000 native plant species. Mountains, river valleys, estuaries and a long coastline add even more variety in a small space.
The islands

The Azores and Madeira belong to **Macaronesia**, a group of Atlantic archipelagos that also includes the Canaries and Cape Verde. Isolation has produced unique species: the Azores bullfinch (priolo), found only in the east of São Miguel, and Zino's petrel on Madeira, one of Europe's rarest seabirds.
The priolo fell to perhaps 40 pairs in the 1990s; restoring its native laurel forest helped it recover to around a thousand birds.
Portugal packs Atlantic, Mediterranean and island worlds into one small country, which makes it unusually rich in life.

cards.title: Peneda-Gerês
cards.text: O único parque nacional de Portugal, criado em 1971, protege montanhas, carvalhais, cavalos garranos, lobos e águias-reais.

deep.x: Peneda-Gerês National Park was created on 8 May 1971 and is still Portugal's only national park. It covers about 700 km² of granite mountains in the far north, between the Minho and Trás-os-Montes, along the border with Galicia.
Who lives there

The **Garrano** is an ancient breed of small, sturdy horse, adapted to steep slopes and harsh winters. Its herds live semi-wild and are a favourite target for wolves, which helps explain why the wolf survives here.
A layered landscape

Ancient oak woods, such as the Mata da Albergaria, shelter roe deer, martens and rare plants like the Gerês iris, which grows wild nowhere else. Stone villages, terraced fields and communal grazing are part of the park too; people have shaped this landscape for thousands of years.
The park also guards Roman roads, prehistoric burial mounds and the traditional granite granaries (espigueiros) of Soajo and Lindoso.

deep.w: Wolves in Gerês are a danger to hikers
deep.r: Iberian wolves avoid people; attacks on humans are virtually unknown in modern times

deep.x: Peneda-Gerês protects not just wild mountains, but a living landscape where wolves, wild horses and villagers share the hills.

cards.title: A Laurissilva da Madeira
cards.text: A floresta laurissilva da Madeira é uma relíquia das florestas que cobriam o sul da Europa há milhões de anos. É Património Mundial da UNESCO desde 1999.

deep.x: Twenty million years ago, much of southern Europe was covered by humid evergreen forest, with trees from the laurel family. As the climate cooled and dried during the ice ages, these forests vanished from the continent. They survived only on the Atlantic islands, where the ocean kept the climate mild and moist.
A forest that drinks clouds

The laurisilva grows on the misty north side of Madeira. Clouds pushed by trade winds drift through the trees, and droplets collect on leaves, moss and lichens and drip to the ground. This "fog capture" adds a lot of water to what falls as rain.
Much of that water ends up in Madeira's **levadas**, narrow irrigation channels built from the 1400s onward, which now double as famous walking trails.
What lives there

x: Trees such as til, vinhático and barbusano, all native to Macaronesia
The Madeira laurel pigeon (trocaz), found only in this forest
The Madeira firecrest, one of Europe's smallest birds
Hundreds of endemic insects, snails, mosses and ferns

deep.x: "Madeira" means "wood" in Portuguese. Early settlers cleared much of the forest by fire; the surviving laurisilva is the largest remaining in the world.
Madeira's laurel forest is a living fossil of Europe's ancient woodland, kept alive by Atlantic clouds.

cards.title: O estuário do Tejo
cards.text: O estuário do Tejo é uma das zonas húmidas mais importantes da Europa para as aves, acolhendo dezenas de milhares de limícolas e flamingos no inverno.

deep.x: Where the Tejo meets the Atlantic, it spreads into a huge inner bay of about 300 km² before squeezing out through a narrow neck at Lisbon. Twice a day the tide drains away to reveal vast mudflats packed with worms, snails and small crustaceans: a buffet for birds.
A stop on a great flyway

The estuary lies on the **East Atlantic Flyway**, a bird migration route from the Arctic to West Africa. Some birds stop to refuel; others spend the whole winter here. In a typical winter, tens of thousands of waders use the estuary, with peak counts of all waterbirds above 100,000.
Why flamingos are pink

Flamingos eat tiny brine shrimp and algae rich in carotenoid pigments, the same family that colours carrots. Their bodies turn those pigments into pink feathers. A flamingo on a poor diet slowly fades to white.
Old salt pans, rice fields and reed beds around Alcochete, Samouco and the EVOA observatory are among the best places to watch. The Tagus Estuary Nature Reserve was created in 1976.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge, finished in 1998 and about 12 km long, was designed and built with measures to reduce disturbance to the birds of the estuary below.
On Lisbon's doorstep, the tide uncovers a feeding ground that keeps tens of thousands of migrating birds alive every winter.

cards.title: Os golfinhos do Sado
cards.text: O estuário do Sado, perto de Setúbal, tem uma população residente de roazes, uma das poucas da Europa, com cerca de 30 animais.

deep.x: Most bottlenose dolphins roam the open sea. The Sado estuary, between Setúbal and the Tróia peninsula, is different: it has a **resident** group that lives there year-round. Only a few places in Europe have resident estuarine dolphins, such as the Shannon estuary in Ireland.
A small, fragile family

Scientists have followed these dolphins since the 1980s and can recognise each one by the nicks and scars on its dorsal fin. The group fell from around 40 to the low 20s by the 2000s, and recent births have brought it back to around 30. With so few animals, every calf matters.

items.b: clicks to find fish in murky water

deep.x: Pressures
Dolphin-watching boats from Setúbal must follow a code: slow down, keep your distance, never surround the animals or chase them, and limit time spent nearby.
Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle as a calf, and others can use it to call that individual, much like a name.
The Sado's resident dolphins are a rare, small family whose survival depends on how we share their busy estuary.

cards.title: As Berlengas
cards.text: O arquipélago das Berlengas, ao largo de Peniche, é uma reserva natural e reserva da biosfera da UNESCO, casa de colónias de aves marinhas e de uma rica vida marinha.

deep.x: About 10 km off Peniche, the Berlengas are a rugged granite archipelago battered by Atlantic swell. The main island, Berlenga Grande, is less than 1.5 km long. The rest are rocky islets called the Estelas and the Farilhões.
Seabird city

Yellow-legged gulls boomed on scraps from fishing boats and landfills and crowded out other species. Managers have reduced their numbers to give rarer seabirds and plants room. The Berlengas were also once the southernmost breeding site of the common guillemot in Europe, though it has nearly disappeared.
Unique life

The islands have plants found nowhere else, such as a Berlengas sea-pink, and their own form of wall lizard. Underwater, the meeting of cold, nutrient-rich water and rocky reefs supports kelp, octopus, sea bream and colourful sea slugs, making it a top diving site.
Since 2019, only about 550 visitors a day may land on Berlenga Grande in summer, to protect its fragile soils and nesting birds.
The Berlengas show that a small, wild island can be both a seabird refuge and a visitor favourite, if access is carefully managed.

cards.title: Sobreiros
cards.text: Portugal é o maior produtor de cortiça do mundo, com cerca de metade da produção mundial. A cortiça é tirada à mão de nove em nove anos sem abater a árvore.

deep.x: Cork is the bark of the cork oak (*Quercus suber*). The tree grows a thick, spongy outer bark to survive fire and drought. Remarkably, it can be stripped without harming the tree, which then grows a new layer.
A slow harvest

Skilled workers strip cork in early summer using axes, when the bark comes away cleanly. A cork oak can live about 200 years, giving around 15 harvests. The first two are too rough for stoppers; good wine corks come from the third stripping onward, when the tree is over 40.

x: First harvest at 25 years
next at 34, then at 43
wine-quality cork from about age 43

deep.x: Why cork works
Cork is made of tiny, sealed cells filled with air, coated in a waxy substance called suberin. That makes it light, waterproof, elastic and a superb insulator.
The montado

Cork oaks grow in open woodlands mixed with pasture, called **montado** in Portugal. This system supports cattle, black pigs, honey and a huge range of wildlife, including the Iberian imperial eagle and the Iberian lynx. It is illegal to fell a cork oak in Portugal without official permission.
The cork oak was declared Portugal's national tree in 2011.
Cork is a renewable harvest that keeps the tree alive and sustains one of Europe's richest farm landscapes.

cards.title: Florestas e fogo
cards.text: As grandes plantações de eucalipto e pinheiro, o abandono dos campos agrícolas e verões mais quentes fizeram dos incêndios uma grande ameaça. Os carvalhos autóctones ardem com menos facilidade.

deep.x: Fire is a natural part of Mediterranean ecosystems, but Portugal's fires have grown more destructive. In 2017, more than 500,000 hectares burnt and over 100 people died, including 66 in the Pedrógão Grande fire in June.
Why the landscape changed

As people left rural villages from the 1960s onward, fields and pastures were abandoned and became dense scrub. Meanwhile, eucalyptus plantations for the paper industry spread fast, along with maritime pine. Eucalyptus is now the most common tree in Portugal's forests, covering roughly a quarter of the area.
Breaking the fire chain

Fires spread fastest across large, continuous blocks of flammable vegetation. A **mosaic** landscape, with farmland, grazing, native woodland and cleared strips around villages, gives fire fewer paths. Portugal now requires landowners to clear vegetation around houses and uses grazing herds and controlled burns in winter to reduce fuel.
Burning eucalyptus bark can peel away in long strips that are carried by the wind, starting new fires hundreds of metres ahead of the main front.
Fire risk is built into the landscape: abandoned land and continuous plantations become fuel when heatwaves arrive.

cards.title: O regresso dos abutres
cards.text: Os grifos e os abutres-pretos regressaram aos parques do Douro Internacional e do Tejo Internacional, graças a campos de alimentação e à proteção.

deep.x: Vultures are nature's clean-up crew. A group of griffons can strip a dead sheep or deer in under an hour, removing carcasses that could otherwise spread disease.
How they nearly vanished

x: Poisoned bait set for wolves and foxes killed many vultures
Food shortages after 2001, when EU rules required farmers to remove dead livestock during the "mad cow" crisis
Disturbance near nesting cliffs

deep.x: The comeback

Rules were relaxed so farmers could leave carcasses at approved **feeding stations**. Poison was tackled with patrols and specially trained dogs. Nesting areas in the Douro International and Tejo International natural parks were protected.

The black vulture, Europe's largest bird of prey with a wingspan up to about 3 m, had stopped breeding in Portugal by the 1970s. It returned to breed in 2010 and now has several small colonies near the Spanish border. Griffons have also increased, and Egyptian vultures arrive in the Douro canyons each spring from Africa.
In South Asia, a cattle painkiller called diclofenac poisoned vultures feeding on carcasses and wiped out more than 95% of some species in the 1990s and 2000s.
Give vultures safe food and protect them from poison, and they return quickly to do their essential clean-up work.

cards.title: Onde ver vida selvagem
cards.text: O Gerês para lobos e cavalos, o estuário do Tejo para flamingos, o Sado para golfinhos, o Douro Internacional para abutres e os Açores para baleias.

deep.x: Portugal is small enough that you can see wolves' tracks in the morning and flamingos by evening, if you plan well. Timing and patience matter more than distance.
Best seasons
More places to try

x: Azores: sperm whales year-round from Pico, Faial and São Miguel; blue whales pass in spring
Ria Formosa near Faro: flamingos, spoonbills and chameleons in the pines
Castro Verde plains, Alentejo: great bustards and lesser kestrels
Berlengas: seabirds, plus diving on reefs

deep.x: Watch well
Wolves are best seen with a specialist guide, and even then often only through tracks, scats or a distant howl. Choose boat operators who follow the official whale and dolphin watching rules.
More than 20 species of whale and dolphin have been recorded around the Azores, making it one of the best places in Europe to see them.
Pick the right season and place, keep your distance, and Portugal's wildlife is closer than you think.

quiz.explain: Criado em 1971.

quiz.q: De quanto em quanto tempo se tira a cortiça de uma árvore?
quiz.explain: A árvore sobrevive.

lessons.title: A comida portuguesa
lessons.summary: Bacalhau, sardinhas, doces conventuais, azeite, queijo, vinho e café.

cards.title: A dieta atlântica

items: Peixe e marisco, muitas vezes grelhados

deep.x: The name was popularised in the 2000s by doctors and nutritionists in Galicia and northern Portugal, to describe how people along the Atlantic edge of Iberia traditionally ate. It is less a set of rules than a portrait of a farming and fishing kitchen.
Built around the sea

Portugal eats more fish per person than any other EU country, about 55–60 kg a year, more than twice the EU average. Sardines, horse mackerel (carapau), hake, octopus and cod are everyday food, not luxuries.
Soup first

A typical meal still starts with soup: caldo verde, made from finely shredded couve galega (a dark leafy cabbage), potatoes and olive oil, or a simple vegetable purée. Bread is on every table, from the dense maize broa of the north to the wheat loaves of the Alentejo.

x: Pulses: chickpeas, broad beans and many kinds of bean
Seasonal vegetables, often from a family plot
Fruit for dessert, with sweets kept for feast days

deep.x: What science says

In 2024 a trial in Galicia found that families who followed the Atlantic diet for six months were less likely to develop metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks for heart disease and diabetes. One study proves little on its own, but it fits a wider pattern: diets rich in fish, vegetables and olive oil tend to be healthy.

deep.w: Portuguese food is simply Mediterranean
deep.r: Portugal is included in UNESCO's Mediterranean diet listing, but it has no Mediterranean coast, and its cooking leans on the Atlantic

deep.x: The Atlantic diet is simple food from the sea and the garden, eaten slowly and together.

cards.text:
Portugal e a Galiza partilham aquilo a que os nutricionistas chamam dieta atlântica: muito peixe, legumes, batatas, pão e azeite, com um pouco de vinho, comidos sem pressa e em família.

Parece-se com a dieta mediterrânica, mas apoia-se mais no mar, na couve e na batata, e em sopas e guisados cozinhados durante horas.

cards.title: Bacalhau

deep.x: Cod lives in cold northern seas. Portuguese sailors were fishing the Grand Banks off Newfoundland soon after 1500. Salt cod suited a Catholic country with many meatless fast days and long sea voyages: it was cheap, light and very hard to spoil.
The White Fleet
Under the Estado Novo, cod fishing became a national campaign to make Portugal self-sufficient. From the 1930s the White Fleet, ships painted white, sailed north each spring for about six months.

x: Each fisherman fished alone from a tiny boat called a dóri, with hand lines
Fog, ice and storms made it one of Europe's most dangerous jobs
A hospital ship, the Gil Eannes, sailed with the fleet; it is now a museum in Viana do Castelo

steps: Dry in the sun at home

deep.x: The fleet faded in the 1970s, as countries extended their fishing zones to 200 nautical miles and cod stocks collapsed. Portugal now imports almost all its cod, much of it from Norway.
From the sea to the plate
Salt cod must be soaked (demolhado) for one to three days, changing the water often, before it is cooked.
Bacalhau à Brás is said to be named after Brás, a tavern keeper in Lisbon's Bairro Alto, though almost nothing is known about him.
Bacalhau is a fish from the far north turned into a Portuguese staple by salt, sun and centuries of habit.

cards.text:
O peixe preferido dos portugueses não vive em águas portuguesas. Os pescadores iam à Terra Nova e à Gronelândia pescar bacalhau e salgavam-no a bordo para que durasse meses.

Hoje a maior parte do bacalhau vem da Noruega e da Islândia, mas a forma portuguesa de o salgar, secar e demolhar continua a ser um ritual nacional.

cards.title: Sardinhas

deep.x: The sardine is a small, oily fish that swims in huge shoals along the Iberian coast. In spring it is thin; through the summer it feeds on plankton and builds up fat. Grilled whole over charcoal with coarse salt, it needs nothing else.
How to eat them

x: Lay a hot sardine on bread, often maize broa in the north
Eat with your fingers, lifting the flesh off the bones
Add a salad of tomato and roasted peppers, and boiled potatoes

deep.x: The canning towns

Canning arrived in the 19th century and boomed during the two world wars, when armies needed food that kept. Setúbal, Matosinhos, Portimão, Olhão and Peniche were lined with factories, where thousands of women cleaned and packed fish by hand on long shifts. Ramirez, founded in 1853, says it is the oldest canning company in the world still working.
Fewer fish, then more

Sardine numbers rise and fall naturally. In the 2010s stocks off Portugal and Spain fell so low that catches were tightly limited for several years. They have since recovered, but scientists and fishermen still watch the quotas closely.
Some fans age tins of sardines for years, like wine, turning them now and then, and say the fish grow softer and richer in the oil.
A sardine is at its best simply grilled in summer, and at its most lasting packed in olive oil.

cards.text:
A sardinha assada é o cheiro do verão português. É melhor mais ou menos de junho a outubro, quando está gorda, e come-se sobre uma fatia de pão que absorve os sucos.

Portugal também é famoso pelas conservas de peixe: as fábricas enlatam sardinha, atum e cavala em azeite desde o século XIX.

cards.title: Pratos regionais

deep.x: Regional cooking follows the land. Where there is rain and grass, there are cows and cabbages; where there are cork-oak plains, there are black pigs; along the coast, there is fish.
North

Porto people are nicknamed tripeiros, "tripe eaters". Legend says that in 1415 the city gave all its meat to the fleet sailing to conquer Ceuta and kept only the offal, creating tripas à moda do Porto, a stew of tripe and white beans. The francesinha, a meat sandwich under melted cheese and a spicy beer-and-tomato sauce, appeared in Porto in the mid-20th century.
Centre
Bairrada, between Coimbra and Aveiro, is known for leitão: suckling pig roasted whole in wood ovens, with crisp skin and a peppery sauce, eaten with the region's sparkling wine.
South
Black Iberian pigs (porco preto) roam the Alentejo's montado, open woodland of cork and holm oaks, and fatten on acorns in autumn.
Islands

deep.w: Pork with clams comes from the Alentejo
deep.r: Despite its name, carne de porco à alentejana is often said to have been created on the coast, pairing Alentejo pork with Algarve clams

deep.x: Portuguese regional food is a map of the landscape: pasture, oak plains, coast and volcano.

cards.text:
Portugal é pequeno, mas cada região cozinha à sua maneira. O norte, verde e chuvoso, come sopas fortes, tripas e enchidos; o centro assa leitão; o Alentejo faz açordas e pratos de porco; o Algarve cozinha peixe e marisco.

As ilhas juntam os seus: o cozido feito no calor vulcânico da terra, nos Açores, e a espetada em pau de louro, na Madeira.

cards.title: Azeite

deep.x: The word azeite comes from the Arabic az-zayt, "the oil". Olive trees have grown here since Roman times or earlier: an olive tree at Mouriscas, near Abrantes, has been estimated by researchers at over 3,000 years old, among the oldest in Europe.
Old groves and new
The Alqueva effect

The Alqueva dam on the Guadiana, completed in 2002, created one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes and brought irrigation to the dry Alentejo. Hedgerow olive groves spread fast, and Portugal went from importing olive oil to exporting it. Critics worry about water use, pesticides and the loss of traditional landscapes.
Grades on the label

x: Acidity here measures free fatty acids, not sourness you can taste
Several regions, such as Trás-os-Montes and Moura, have protected-origin (DOP) oils
Light and heat spoil oil, so dark bottles and cool cupboards help

deep.w: You shouldn't fry with extra virgin olive oil
deep.r: Its smoke point, around 190–210 °C, is above normal frying temperatures, and it is quite stable when heated

deep.x: Portugal's olive oil boom joined ancient trees with modern irrigation, bringing real gains and real trade-offs.

cards.text:
O azeite é a gordura da cozinha portuguesa. Tempera o peixe e as batatas cozidas, termina as sopas e é regado generosamente sobre o bacalhau.

Portugal tornou-se um dos principais produtores mundiais, sobretudo graças aos novos olivais de regadio do Alentejo. Variedades tradicionais como a Galega e a Cobrançosa dão azeites que vão do suave ao picante.

cards.title: Queijo

deep.x: The thistle is the cardoon, a wild relative of the artichoke. Its dried purple flowers are soaked and crushed, and the liquid, rich in plant enzymes, curdles the milk. This method is rare outside Portugal and Spain.
How Serra da Estrela is made

It is made from late autumn to spring around the Serra da Estrela, mainland Portugal's highest range, from the milk of local sheep breeds. When ripe, the paste is so soft that the top crust is cut off like a lid and the cheese is scooped out with a spoon. Aged longer, as Serra da Estrela Velho, it becomes firm and sharp.
Across the country

x: Azeitão: small, creamy ewe's cheese from the Arrábida hills
Nisa and Évora: firmer ewe's cheeses from the Alentejo
São Jorge: a hard cow's milk cheese, sharp and peppery
Requeijão: a fresh whey cheese, often eaten with pumpkin jam

deep.x: The Azores have roughly as many cows as people and produce about a third of Portugal's milk, much of it from cows grazing outdoors all year.
In Portugal a wild thistle, not a calf's stomach, turns sheep's milk into some of Europe's most distinctive cheese.

cards.text:
Os queijos portugueses mais conhecidos são feitos com leite de ovelha e coalhados não com coalho animal, mas com a flor de um cardo silvestre. O resultado é muitas vezes mole, cremoso e ligeiramente amargo.

O Serra da Estrela é o mais famoso, mas o Azeitão, o Nisa, o Évora e o São Jorge, dos Açores, também têm denominação protegida.

cards.title: Doçaria conventual

deep.x: From the 15th century, sugar from Madeira and later Brazil made Portugal one of the first European countries where sugar was fairly plentiful. Convents had eggs from their farms, sugar from the trade, time and skill. They sold sweets to raise money or gave them to benefactors.
Names with a wink
When the convents closed

In 1834, after the Liberal Wars, religious orders for men were abolished and their property sold; convents for women could stay open until their last nun died. Recipes passed to families and bakeries. In 1837 a shop beside the Jerónimos Monastery began selling the custard tarts now known as pastéis de Belém, from a recipe still kept secret.
Nata or Belém?

Only the Belém shop can call its tarts pastéis de Belém; everywhere else they are pastéis de nata. Both have flaky, rolled pastry and a custard of egg yolks, milk and sugar, scorched in a very hot oven and dusted with cinnamon if you like.

x: Aveiro: ovos moles in shell-shaped wafers
Sintra: queijadas and travesseiros
Tentúgal, near Coimbra: paper-thin pastries filled with egg cream

deep.x: Ovos moles de Aveiro were the first Portuguese pastry to receive EU protected status, in 2008.
Portugal's sweets are the sweet side of history: sugar from the empire, eggs from the farm and patience from the cloister.

cards.text:
Muitos doces portugueses nasceram em conventos e mosteiros. Freiras e frades usavam as claras de ovo para engomar a roupa e clarificar o vinho, e sobravam montanhas de gemas, que misturavam com açúcar da Madeira e do Brasil.

Os resultados têm nomes celestiais: toucinho do céu, papos de anjo, barriga de freira. O pastel de nata é o herdeiro mais famoso desta tradição.

cards.title: Regiões vinícolas

deep.x: Vinho Verde

The region in the green north-west, demarcated in 1908, is one of the largest in Europe. Its best-known grape is Alvarinho, grown around Monção and Melgaço on the Minho river. Light, fairly low in alcohol and sometimes slightly fizzy, the wines suit fish and seafood.

deep.w: Vinho Verde is made from green grapes
deep.r: "Verde" means young: the wine is meant to be drunk fresh, and it can be white, red or rosé

deep.x: Douro

The Douro's vineyards climb steep schist slopes, cut into terraces by hand over centuries. Summers are very hot, and vine roots push deep into cracks in the rock to find water. Port is made here and traditionally aged in Vila Nova de Gaia, opposite Porto, while unfortified Douro reds and whites have become famous in their own right.
Alentejo
In the south, wide plains, hot summers and large estates give rich, fruity reds. The Alentejo also keeps a Roman method alive: vinho de talha, fermented in huge clay jars.
More to explore

x: Dão: elegant reds from granite hills
Bairrada: Baga reds and sparkling wines
Madeira and Setúbal: fortified and sweet wines

deep.x: The Portuguese drink more wine per person than almost any other nation, about 60 litres a year per adult.
Climate, soil and native grapes make Portugal's wine map one of the most varied in Europe.

cards.text:
Portugal reúne vinhos muito diferentes num país pequeno. No chuvoso Minho, o Vinho Verde é leve e fresco. Subindo o vale do Douro, as encostas de xisto em socalcos dão o vinho do Porto e tintos encorpados. Nas planícies quentes do Alentejo, os vinhos são maduros e macios.

A maioria é feita com castas autóctones que quase não existem noutro lado, como o Alvarinho, a Touriga Nacional e o Antão Vaz.

cards.title: A cultura do café

items.b: café com muito leite, em copo

deep.x: Coffee became popular in Portugal in the 18th century, and the empire supplied it: Brazil, then São Tomé, Angola and Timor. In the early 1970s Angola was one of the world's largest producers, and its robusta beans shaped the strong Portuguese blend, which usually mixes arabica and robusta.
Beyond the bica
The Porto word cimbalino comes from La Cimbali, an Italian brand of espresso machine that spread through the city's cafés.
Historic cafés

x: A Brasileira (1905), in Chiado, with a bronze Fernando Pessoa at a table outside
Majestic (1921), on Porto's Rua de Santa Catarina, all mirrors and carved wood
Nicola, on Rossio, a writers' café since the 18th century, rebuilt in art deco style in 1929

deep.x: A coffee town

Campo Maior, in the Alentejo near the Spanish border, is home to Delta, Portugal's biggest coffee brand, founded by Rui Nabeiro in 1961. The town grew around roasting, and it now has a coffee science museum.

deep.w: "Bica" stands for "Beba Isto Com Açúcar"
deep.r: It's a popular story with no evidence; "bica" also means a spout, and the word's real origin is uncertain

deep.x: In Portugal coffee is less a drink than a short pause, taken standing up, many times a day.

cards.text:
Em Portugal, um café é um expresso curto e forte, bebido de pé ao balcão em um ou dois minutos, muitas vezes várias vezes ao dia. Em Lisboa é uma bica, no Porto um cimbalino.

Os cafés e as pastelarias são as salas de estar do bairro. O café é barato, normalmente 1 € ou menos, e torrado num estilo escuro e suave marcado pelas ligações de Portugal ao Brasil e a África.

cards.title: A tempura e mais além

deep.x: Portuguese traders first landed in Japan in 1543, on the island of Tanegashima. Nagasaki became their main port from 1571. For almost a century, until they were expelled in 1639, Portuguese merchants and Jesuit missionaries brought goods, guns and recipes.
The batter story

The most quoted origin of the name is the Latin quattuor tempora, Portuguese têmporas: four short seasons of fasting in the Church year, when fish and vegetables replaced meat. Other words have been suggested, such as tempero (seasoning), so the origin isn't certain. Japanese cooks later made the batter thinner and crisper.
Other traces in Japan
Around the world

x: Goa: vindaloo, from vinha d'alhos, a wine and garlic marinade
Macau: Macanese cooking mixes Portuguese, Chinese and Malay flavours
Malacca: Kristang families of Portuguese descent still cook "devil's curry"

deep.w: "Arigatō" comes from "obrigado"
deep.r: The Japanese word existed long before the Portuguese arrived; the likeness is a coincidence

deep.x: Portuguese sailors carried recipes as well as spices, and some, like tempura, became famous under new names.

cards.text:
A tempura japonesa deve provavelmente a sua origem aos mercadores e missionários portugueses, que chegaram ao Japão na década de 1540. Fritavam peixe e legumes em polme, tal como os peixinhos da horta, feijão-verde panado à portuguesa.

O nome pode vir das têmporas, os dias de jejum em que os católicos evitavam a carne. A cozinha portuguesa também deixou a sua marca em Goa, Macau, Malaca e no Brasil.

quiz.q: O que coalha o leite do queijo Serra da Estrela?
quiz.explain: A flor do cardo coalha o leite de ovelha.

quiz.q: O que significa "verde" em Vinho Verde?
quiz.explain: É um vinho jovem e pode ser branco, tinto ou rosé.

quiz.explain: O bacalhau vive nos mares frios do norte.
