lessons.title: Ciência e invenção portuguesas
lessons.summary: Dos instrumentos dos navegadores aos laboratórios modernos: os cientistas portugueses e o que descobriram.

cards.title: Ciência para o mar

deep.x: Longitude, a ship's east–west position, could not be measured reliably at sea until the 18th century. Latitude was easier, because the height of a star above the horizon changes as you sail north or south. Portuguese pilots began using this from about the 1450s–1460s, as voyages pushed down the coast of Africa.
From star to Sun

In the north, the Pole Star sits almost above the North Pole, so its height in degrees roughly equals your latitude. But it sinks towards the horizon near the equator and vanishes south of it. Pilots therefore switched to the Sun at midday, which needed a table of its changing daily position, called its declination.

x: Noon Sun 60° high, due south
Declination that day 10° north
Latitude = 90° − 60° + 10° = 40° N, near Aveiro

deep.x: Tools of the trade

x: The **quadrant**, a quarter circle with a plumb line, measured the Pole Star
The **mariner's astrolabe**, a heavy open bronze wheel, resisted the wind on a rolling deck
The **cross-staff** (balestilha) let a pilot sight the horizon and a star at once

deep.x: The rules were printed in the "Regiment of the Astrolabe and Quadrant", whose oldest surviving copy dates from about 1509. Its Sun tables drew on Abraão Zacuto, a Jewish astronomer whose Almanach Perpetuum was printed in Leiria in 1496.
An astrolabe from the Esmeralda, a ship of Vasco da Gama's second voyage that sank off Oman in 1503, is thought to be the oldest mariner's astrolabe ever found.
Portuguese navigation turned astronomy into a routine any trained pilot could follow with a table and an instrument.

cards.text:
Longe da vista de terra, os pilotos portugueses do século XV precisavam de saber quão a norte ou a sul estavam. Determinavam a latitude medindo a altura da Estrela Polar ou do Sol ao meio-dia.

Instrumentos simples, regimentos impressos e tábuas astronómicas tornaram isto numa rotina que qualquer piloto podia aprender.

cards.title: O nónio de Pedro Nunes

deep.x: An astrolabe or quadrant usually showed whole degrees. Dividing them further made the marks too crowded to read. Nunes described his solution in De crepusculis, a 1542 book on the length of twilight, as a tool for astronomers and pilots alike.
How the nonius worked

Inside the main quarter circle he drew dozens of smaller concentric arcs. The outer one was split into 90 equal parts, the next into 89, the next into 88, and so on. When the sighting arm fell between marks on one arc, it would land almost exactly on a mark of another. Knowing which arc and which mark, a short calculation gave the angle to a fraction of a degree.

steps: Find the arc with a hit

deep.x: From nonius to vernier

Engraving dozens of arcs accurately was hard, and the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe found it impractical. In 1631 the French engineer Pierre Vernier replaced the arcs with a single small sliding scale. The principle is the same: compare two scales with slightly different spacing.

x: Main scale marked in mm
10 vernier marks span 9 mm, so each is 0.9 mm
The mark that lines up gives tenths: 0.1 mm precision

deep.x: In German and Portuguese the sliding scale on a calliper is still called a Nonius or nónio, after Nunes' Latin name, Petrus Nonius.
Two scales with slightly different spacing reveal what neither shows alone: that was Nunes' gift to every workshop.

cards.text:
Em 1542, o matemático Pedro Nunes propôs uma forma engenhosa de ler ângulos com mais precisão do que as marcas de um instrumento permitiam.

A sua ideia, o nónio, usava muitas escalas concêntricas. Simplificada um século depois, sobrevive na escala vernier de qualquer craveira.

cards.title: Garcia de Orta

deep.x: Orta studied medicine at Salamanca and Alcalá in Spain, taught briefly in Lisbon and sailed to India in 1534 as a ship's doctor. He settled in Goa, treated viceroys and ordinary patients, and grew many of the plants he wrote about in his own garden. He also held a lease on land on the island of Bombay, today's Mumbai.
A book of conversations

His "Colloquies on the Simples and Drugs of India" is a series of conversations between Orta and an imaginary visiting doctor, Ruano. The visitor quotes the ancient Greek and Arab authorities; Orta often replies that experience shows otherwise. It was one of the first books printed in India with European type.
Across Europe
In 1567 the Flemish botanist Carolus Clusius published a Latin summary, which was reprinted and translated many times. For about a century it was a standard European reference on Asian medicines.
A tragic ending

Orta came from a family of New Christians, Jews forced to convert. After his death in 1568 the Inquisition, newly active in Goa, pursued his family; his sister Catarina was burned in 1569. In 1580 his own remains were dug up and burned.
A garden in Lisbon's Parque das Nações and a Portuguese scientific journal both bear his name.
Orta put first-hand observation ahead of ancient authority, at a time when that could be dangerous.

cards.text:
Garcia de Orta foi um médico português que viveu em Goa mais de 30 anos. Em 1563 publicou os Colóquios, um livro sobre as plantas medicinais e as drogas da Ásia.

Escrito em diálogos vivos, punha à prova as velhas afirmações com aquilo que via, provava e aprendia com os curandeiros locais.

cards.title: A máquina voadora de Gusmão

deep.x: Gusmão was born in 1685 in Santos, in Portuguese Brazil, and studied at Coimbra. In 1709 he petitioned the king for exclusive rights to a machine for travelling through the air. The court was intrigued, and he was asked to demonstrate.
The demonstration

Accounts describe several trials at the royal palace in early August 1709. In the best known, a small balloon of thick paper, with a flame burning in a bowl beneath it, rose a few metres before servants knocked it down for fear it would set the curtains alight.
The Passarola

A famous drawing shows a bird-like ship with wings, a sail and a canopy. Historians think the drawing was at least partly fanciful, perhaps even meant to mislead rivals, rather than a working design. No reliable record says it flew.

items.r: Only a small hot-air model rose

deep.x: A quiet end
Gusmão later fell under suspicion from the Inquisition, fled to Spain and died in Toledo in 1724. The Montgolfier brothers' first public balloon flight in France came only in 1783.
José Saramago's novel Memorial do Convento (1982) brings Gusmão and his Passarola to life, and in the story the machine really flies.
Gusmão showed that hot air could lift an object, three generations before ballooning took off.

cards.text:
Em agosto de 1709, Bartolomeu de Gusmão, um padre nascido no Brasil, mostrou a D. João V um pequeno balão de papel que subia com ar quente, numa sala em Lisboa.

Também desenhou uma aeronave em forma de pássaro, a Passarola. Quase de certeza nunca voou, mas tornou-o famoso como "o Padre Voador".

cards.title: Egas Moniz: Nobel e polémica

items.b: um caso de estudo em ética

deep.x: Born António Caetano de Abreu Freire in 1874, he took the name Egas Moniz from a medieval nobleman. Before medicine made him famous he was a member of parliament, ambassador to Spain and briefly foreign minister, and in 1919 he led Portugal's delegation at the Paris Peace Conference.
Why it seemed promising

In the 1930s asylums were overcrowded and there were almost no effective treatments for severe psychosis or depression. In 1935–36 Moniz and the surgeon Pedro Almeida Lima operated on about 20 patients and reported that most improved. To many doctors, any hope looked better than none.
What was missing

x: Small numbers and no comparison group
Short follow-up, often weeks rather than years
"Improvement" often meant calmer and easier to manage
Patients were rarely able to give real consent

deep.x: Today new treatments must pass controlled trials and ethics committees, and patients must give informed consent, following principles set out in the Nuremberg Code (1947) and the Declaration of Helsinki (1964).

deep.w: Moniz invented the "ice-pick" lobotomy
deep.r: That crude version was spread in the USA by Walter Freeman; Moniz's operation was done in theatre by a surgeon

deep.x: A Nobel Prize recognises a discovery as judged at the time; good science keeps testing it afterwards.

cards.text:
Egas Moniz, neurologista e político, ganhou o primeiro Prémio Nobel português em 1949 pela leucotomia, uma operação ao cérebro para doenças mentais graves.

A operação foi depois abandonada, e o prémio ainda hoje é discutido. A sua história é usada agora para ensinar como a medicina deve testar novos tratamentos.

cards.title: Abel Salazar

deep.x: Born in Guimarães, Salazar graduated in medicine in Porto in 1915 and soon became professor of histology, the study of tissues. He built a laboratory and a school of young researchers, working especially on the structure of the ovary.
A new stain

Cells are mostly transparent, so histologists colour them with chemicals. Salazar developed a method using tannin and then iron salts, known as the tano-ferric method, which revealed fine structures inside cells. It earned him recognition from scientists abroad.
Silenced

Salazar spoke and wrote for free thought, science education and social justice. In 1935 the Estado Novo regime dismissed him and several other professors. For years he could not teach, and he turned more and more to painting and writing.
The artist
His paintings and drawings show working people: washerwomen, fishermen, labourers and market women, drawn with sympathy and energy.

items.b: his home, São Mamede de Infesta

deep.x: A saying attributed to him is still quoted to medical students: a doctor who only knows medicine doesn't even know medicine.
Abel Salazar believed a scientist should also be a citizen and an artist, and he paid a price for it.

cards.text:
Abel Salazar (1889–1946) foi um médico e investigador do Porto que estudou tecidos ao microscópio e inventou um método de coloração.

Foi também pintor e escritor. Em 1935, a ditadura afastou-o da universidade pelas suas ideias. Não tinha qualquer parentesco com o ditador Salazar.

cards.title: A ciência depois de 1974

deep.x: In the early 1970s Portugal had one of the lowest numbers of researchers per person in Western Europe, and its universities were small. Joining the European Community in 1986 brought funds and partners, and the same year Portugal joined CERN, the particle physics laboratory near Geneva.
The Mariano Gago years

The physicist José Mariano Gago became Portugal's first Minister of Science in 1995 and held the post again from 2005 to 2011. His government created the Foundation for Science and Technology (FCT) in 1997 to fund projects and grants, and launched Ciência Viva to bring science to the public.
A new generation

x: Doctoral and postdoctoral grants sent thousands abroad, and many came back
New institutes grew around universities in Lisbon, Porto, Coimbra, Braga and Aveiro
Women make up over 40% of Portugal's researchers, more than the EU average
R&D about 0.5% of GDP in 1990
about 1.7% in 2022
more than three times the share, though still below the EU's ~2.2%

deep.x: In 1993 Portugal launched its first satellite, PoSAT-1, a small microsatellite built with British partners.
In a few decades Portugal went from a science latecomer to a country with a dense web of researchers and labs.

cards.text:
Durante a ditadura, poucos portugueses faziam investigação. Depois do regresso da democracia em 1974, e sobretudo a partir dos anos 90, Portugal investiu fortemente na ciência.

A despesa em investigação mais do que triplicou em percentagem da economia, e milhares de jovens receberam bolsas para fazer doutoramentos em Portugal e no estrangeiro.

cards.title: Ciência Viva

deep.x: The programme began in 1996 with a simple idea: science should be done, not just read about. Early projects paid for experiments in school classrooms. Today the agency also supports school science clubs and links pupils with research labs.
The centres

Each centre has its own theme, often tied to its region: astronomy, the sea, forests, energy or geology. The Pavilhão do Conhecimento, opened in 1999 in the Parque das Nações, welcomes large numbers of school groups and families every year.
Science in summer

Each summer, "Ciência Viva no Verão" offers free or low-cost activities led by scientists: night-sky observations, geology walks, birdwatching and visits to labs and lighthouses. Many are booked online and fill quickly.

x: Secondary pupils can spend a week or two of their holidays working in real research labs
Families can join researchers on field trips across the country

deep.x: During Expo '98 the Pavilhão building, designed by architect João Luís Carrilho da Graça, was the Pavilion of the Knowledge of the Seas.
Ciência Viva's idea is that people who have done an experiment themselves understand and enjoy science more.

cards.text:
A Ciência Viva, criada em 1996, é a agência portuguesa para a difusão da cultura científica. Gere uma rede de cerca de 20 centros de ciência, de Bragança ao Algarve e às ilhas.

A sua casa-mãe é o Pavilhão do Conhecimento, em Lisboa, um museu de ciência interativo num edifício da Expo '98.

cards.title: A Fundação Champalimaud

deep.x: António de Sommer Champalimaud (1918–2004) built a business empire in cement, steel, banking and insurance, lost much of it in the nationalisations of 1975 and rebuilt it later. In his will he asked for a foundation dedicated to biomedical research. Leonor Beleza, a former health minister, has led it since its creation.
A building on the river

The Centre for the Unknown, designed by the Indian architect Charles Correa, stands where the Tagus meets the sea, close to where the navigators set sail. Its name links today's exploration of the brain and body to the voyages of discovery.
What it does

Hundreds of scientists from dozens of countries work there. Neuroscientists study how animals and people make decisions, move and learn, often with mice and fruit flies. The clinic combines treatment with research, so that new methods can reach patients faster.
A prize for sight

Champalimaud wanted to fight blindness. The António Champalimaud Vision Award, worth €1 million, is among the largest prizes in science. In alternate years it rewards research and work against blindness in developing countries.
The Champalimaud Foundation shows how private money can build world-class science when it is given for the long term.

cards.text:
Quando o industrial António Champalimaud morreu, em 2004, deixou cerca de um quarto da sua fortuna, à volta de 500 milhões de euros, para criar uma fundação de investigação médica.

O seu Centro Champalimaud para o Desconhecido, inaugurado em 2010 junto ao Tejo, em Belém, estuda o cérebro e o cancro e trata doentes.

cards.title: A investigação hoje

deep.x: Research in Portugal is spread across universities and their institutes, state laboratories, private foundations and, increasingly, companies. Most public money comes from the FCT and from the European Union's research programmes.
Strengths

x: Ocean and marine science, from the Azores to the deep Atlantic
Biomedicine and neuroscience in Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra
Materials and nanotechnology, including the Iberian Nanotechnology Laboratory in Braga, run jointly with Spain since 2009

deep.x: Into space

In 2019 Portugal created its own space agency, Portugal Space. Portuguese companies make parts for European rockets and satellites, and in 2024 ISTSat-1, a small satellite built by students at Lisbon's Instituto Superior Técnico, flew on the first launch of the Ariane 6 rocket.
Challenges

Researchers often work on short contracts, salaries are lower than in northern Europe, and many trained scientists leave. Keeping them, or attracting them back, remains a central aim of science policy.
Portuguese science is now international by design, with labs that train and attract researchers from around the world.

cards.text:
Os cientistas portugueses trabalham hoje em áreas que vão das neurociências e do cancro às ciências do mar, aos materiais e ao espaço. Muitos institutos acolhem equipas internacionais.

Portugal é membro do CERN, da Agência Espacial Europeia e do Observatório Europeu do Sul, e os seus investigadores ganham bolsas europeias competitivas.

quiz.q: O que ajudava o nónio de Pedro Nunes os navegadores e astrónomos a fazer?
quiz.explain: Inspirou a escala vernier das craveiras.

quiz.q: Quem mostrou a D. João V um pequeno balão de ar quente em 1709?
quiz.explain: Subiu 74 anos antes do voo público dos irmãos Montgolfier.

quiz.q: Porque recebeu Egas Moniz o Prémio Nobel de 1949?
quiz.explain: A operação foi depois abandonada, e o prémio ainda hoje é discutido.

quiz.q: Que agência, criada em 1996, gere a rede portuguesa de centros de ciência?
quiz.explain: A sua casa-mãe é o Pavilhão do Conhecimento, em Lisboa.

lessons.title: Festas e tradições
lessons.summary: O Carnaval, a Páscoa, os Santos Populares, as romarias, o Natal e a saudade.

cards.title: Carnaval

deep.x: Carnaval is the last party before the 40 days of Lent, traditionally a time of fasting. Its spirit is the world turned upside down: masks, men dressed as women, mockery of the powerful and, in villages, battles with flour, water or eggs.
The caretos of Podence

In Podence, near Macedo de Cavaleiros, young men become caretos and charge noisily through the streets. UNESCO added the Carnival of Podence to its intangible heritage list in 2019. Similar masked figures appear across Trás-os-Montes and in Galicia, and some link them with old winter rites.
Satire in Torres Vedras

Torres Vedras calls its carnival, held since 1923, "the most Portuguese in Portugal". It avoids samba; instead, giant figures and floats mock politicians and celebrities, and groups of men dressed as women, the matrafonas, fill the streets.
Samba by the sea
Ovar, Mealhada, Loulé, Sesimbra and Funchal stage large parades with samba schools and floats inspired by Rio de Janeiro. Loulé's, from 1906, is among the oldest in the country.
Shrove Tuesday is not a public holiday: each year the government decides whether to give its staff the day off, and many employers follow.
Carnaval turns the world upside down for a few days, from masked caretos to satirical floats.

cards.text:
Antes da Quaresma vem o Carnaval, ou Entrudo. As terras fazem desfiles, as crianças mascaram-se e a Terça-feira de Carnaval é muitas vezes dia de folga, embora não seja feriado oficial.

Os velhos costumes rurais sobrevivem lado a lado com o samba à brasileira. Em Podence, em Trás-os-Montes, os caretos mascarados, com fatos de franjas de lã coloridas, correm pela aldeia a abanar chocalhos.

cards.title: As tradições da Páscoa

deep.x: For practising Catholics, Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus and ends the 40 days of Lent. For many less religious families too, it is a time for shared meals, sugared almonds and roast lamb or kid. Good Friday is a national public holiday.
Holy Week in Braga

Braga, an archbishop's seat since early medieval times, has Portugal's best-known Holy Week. In the Ecce Homo procession on the Thursday night, barefoot hooded figures called farricocos carry torches and rattles through the dark streets.
The compasso

In the Minho and other northern areas, a group led by a priest or lay members of the parish goes from house to house with a cross. Families who want the visit leave their door open and cover the floor with flowers.
Folar
Tradition says godchildren take a gift to their godparents on Palm Sunday, and receive a folar in return at Easter.

x: Sugared almonds (amêndoas) in pastel colours fill shop windows
Roast lamb or kid (cabrito) is the classic Easter lunch

deep.x: Easter Sunday can fall anywhere between 22 March and 25 April: it is the Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox.
Portuguese Easter mixes solemn processions with open doors, shared tables and gifts between godparents and godchildren.

cards.text:
A Páscoa é uma grande festa de família em Portugal, sobretudo no norte. Em Braga, a Semana Santa traz procissões noturnas solenes que atraem milhares de visitantes.

No Domingo de Páscoa, muitas aldeias recebem o compasso, uma pequena procissão que visita as casas com a cruz. Os padrinhos dão aos afilhados o folar, um pão de Páscoa doce ou salgado.

cards.title: Santo António

items: Toda a noite: arraiais na Alfama

deep.x: Santo António was born Fernando de Bulhões in Lisbon, near the cathedral, where a church now stands on the site of his family's house. He took the name António when he joined the Franciscans.
Thrones and coins

In the past, children built little altars to the saint, the tronos de Santo António, on doorsteps and asked passers-by for "a little coin for Santo António". The custom is said to date from collections to rebuild his church after 1755, and it has been revived in some neighbourhoods and schools.
The weddings

The Casamentos de Santo António began in 1958, sponsored by a newspaper for couples who could not afford a wedding. They stopped after 1974 and were revived by the city in 1997. Today a group of couples marry on the saint's day, in religious or civil ceremonies, and parade through the city.
The sardine as symbol
The sardine has become the festival's emblem. Each year Lisbon holds a design competition for sardine illustrations, which appear on posters, shop windows and souvenirs.

deep.w: Santo António is Lisbon's official patron saint
deep.r: The official patron is São Vicente, whose relics came to Lisbon in 1173; Santo António is the people's favourite

deep.x: On Santo António's night Lisbon becomes one long neighbourhood party, led by a saint who matches couples and finds lost things.

cards.text:
O santo preferido de Lisboa é Santo António. Na noite de 12 de junho, todos os bairros históricos se transformam num arraial, uma festa de rua com sardinhas assadas, bifanas, cerveja e música.

O santo é conhecido como casamenteiro e como quem encontra as coisas perdidas, e todos os anos a cidade celebra casamentos em seu nome.

cards.title: São João

deep.x: The feast of Saint John the Baptist falls on 24 June, close to the summer solstice. Across Europe, midsummer night was linked with fire, water and herbs, and Porto keeps traces of these older customs.
Night rituals

items: Give a pot of manjerico basil

x: Cascatas sanjoaninas are miniature scenes of town life around a statue of the saint, built by neighbourhoods and judged in contests
Paper hot-air balloons with a flame inside are now restricted, because they can start fires
Roast lamb with potatoes is a classic lunch on the 24th

deep.x: The regatta

On 24 June the port wine houses race their rabelo boats, the flat-bottomed sailing boats once used to bring barrels of port down the Douro to Gaia. It is a reminder of the time before roads, railways and dams, when the river was the only highway.
Porto and Braga
Both cities make the 24th a municipal holiday, so people can sleep after the long night.
The plastic hammers appeared only in the 1960s, but they spread so fast that they now feel as old as the festival itself.
São João is midsummer night, Porto style: fire in the sky, a hammer on the head and the sea at dawn.

cards.text:
O São João é a maior noite do Porto. A 23 de junho, a cidade fica na rua até de madrugada, a dar marteladas na cabeça de desconhecidos com martelinhos de plástico, a agitar alhos-porros, a assar sardinhas e a comer caldo verde.

À meia-noite, o fogo de artifício rebenta sobre o Douro. Depois, muita gente caminha até ao mar, na Foz, para esperar o nascer do sol. Braga também faz um enorme São João.

cards.title: São Pedro

deep.x: In the Gospels, Peter was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee, and he is traditionally the keeper of the keys of heaven. Portuguese fishing communities adopted him as a protector, alongside local devotions to the Virgin Mary.
Póvoa de Varzim

Póvoa, north of Porto, was one of the main fishing towns of the north. On São Pedro night its neighbourhoods, each with its own colours, compete for the best decorations and the best rusga, and the whole town stays up late. The 29th is the town's municipal holiday.
The June saints together
Bonfires, herbs and dew gathered on these nights were once believed to bring health, luck or a future husband. Many people now enjoy them simply as fun.
By the sea

x: Boats are decorated, and in some harbours blessed
Grilled sardines and other fish are the classic food
Fireworks over the water end the night

deep.x: Póvoa's fishermen used siglas poveiras, simple carved family marks, to sign boats, tools and even gravestones, a kind of signature for people who often could not read or write.
São Pedro ends the June saints by the sea, with fishing towns turning out in their best.

cards.text:
O São Pedro, a 29 de junho, fecha o mês dos Santos Populares. Como São Pedro era pescador, a sua festa é mais forte nas terras do litoral.

Na Póvoa de Varzim, os bairros competem com ruas enfeitadas, cascatas e rusgas, grupos de cantores e dançarinos vestidos de pescadores. Sintra, o Montijo e Évora também fazem grandes feiras de São Pedro.

cards.title: Romarias

deep.x: The word comes from romeiro, originally a pilgrim to Rome. Many romarias began as gatherings at isolated hilltop chapels, where people came from miles around and stayed for food, music and dancing after the service.
What happens

Some pilgrims keep a promessa, a promise made in a time of need, by walking the last stretch or bringing candles. For many others the romaria is mainly a reunion with family and neighbours, including emigrants who time their summer visit home around it.
Famous romarias
In Viana, women in traditional dress parade wearing layers of gold, and fishermen carry the image of the Virgin to the sea.
Giants and big heads

Gigantones, giant figures several metres tall, and cabeçudos, figures with enormous heads, dance through the crowds. Zés Pereiras, bands of big bass drums, sometimes with bagpipes, wake the town at dawn.
Every four years in Tomar, at the Festa dos Tabuleiros, young women carry trays of bread on their heads as tall as themselves; the last was in 2023.
A romaria joins the sacred and the festive: a procession in the morning, a party until late at night.

cards.text:
Uma romaria é uma festa construída em torno de uma peregrinação a uma capela ou santuário. Mistura a procissão religiosa com a feira: bandas filarmónicas, bombos, ranchos folclóricos, bancas de doces e fogo de artifício.

O verão é a época das romarias, sobretudo no norte. A Senhora d'Agonia, em Viana do Castelo, em agosto, é uma das maiores, com ruas atapetadas de serradura colorida e flores.

cards.title: As festas de outono

deep.x: Pão por Deus

Children carry small cloth bags and recite rhymes at each door. In Lisbon a story links the custom with 1755, when the earthquake struck on All Saints' Day and survivors begged for food. In some regions it has other names, such as bolinho. The next day, All Souls', many families visit cemeteries and bring flowers to their relatives' graves.

deep.w: Pão por Deus is a copy of Halloween
deep.r: The Portuguese custom is centuries old and independent; Halloween has spread more recently alongside it

deep.x: The legend of São Martinho

Martin was a 4th-century Roman soldier. On a stormy day he met a freezing beggar and cut his cloak in two to share it. Legend says the sun came out at once, the origin of the few mild days often seen in November. He later became bishop of Tours, in France.
The magusto

items: Fire, clay pot or old drum

deep.x: Chestnuts were a staple food in the north and centre before potatoes arrived from the Americas. Água-pé is a light drink made by adding water to pressed grape skins, and jeropiga is sweet grape juice strengthened with spirit. A popular saying sends everyone to the cellar on São Martinho's day to taste the new wine.
All Saints' Day was dropped as a public holiday in 2013, during the financial crisis, and restored in 2016.
Portugal's autumn feasts are about sharing: bread at the door on 1 November, chestnuts round the fire on the 11th.

cards.text:
A 1 de novembro, Dia de Todos os Santos, em muitas terras as crianças vão de porta em porta pedir o "pão por Deus" e recebem pão, frutos secos, maçãs e doces.

A 11 de novembro, dia de São Martinho, as famílias juntam-se para o magusto: castanhas assadas na fogueira, com vinho novo. Os dias amenos que costumam vir por essa altura chamam-se "verão de São Martinho".

cards.title: O Natal e a consoada

deep.x: Consoada comes from consolar, "to comfort": originally a light meal on a fast day, before the Christmas feast. Because the eve was a meatless day in the Catholic calendar, fish became the tradition. In parts of the north, octopus joins or replaces the cod. Midnight Mass is called the Missa do Galo, the "rooster's Mass".
The sweet table

items.b: fried bread in syrup or wine

deep.x: Bolo-rei

The bolo-rei (king cake), crowned with candied fruit, came from France in the 19th century; Lisbon's Confeitaria Nacional is said to have introduced it around 1870. It used to hide a dried broad bean and a small gift: whoever found the bean paid for next year's cake. The gift was dropped for safety reasons, and many bakeries now leave out the bean too.
Fires and songs

items: Madeiro: log fire in the square

deep.x: In villages of the Beira and Trás-os-Montes, young people gather a huge pile of logs, the madeiro, in the church square and light it on Christmas Eve; it may burn for days. On the 25th, leftover cod is fried with cabbage and potatoes as roupa velha, "old clothes".
In parts of the north, families used to leave the consoada table laid overnight, with food for the souls of relatives who had died.
Consoada puts the humble salt cod at the centre of Portugal's most important family meal.

cards.text:
A principal refeição de Natal em Portugal é a consoada, na noite de 24 de dezembro. A ementa clássica é bacalhau cozido com couves, batatas e ovos, tudo regado com azeite e alho.

Depois vêm doces como as rabanadas, os sonhos e as filhoses, e muitas famílias abrem os presentes à meia-noite. O bolo-rei, um bolo em forma de coroa com frutas cristalizadas, fica na mesa até 6 de janeiro.

cards.title: O galo de Barcelos

deep.x: Barcelos potters once made mostly practical ware: pots, jugs and roof tiles, sold at the town's great weekly market. Small figures and clay whistles were a sideline for children and fairs, and they grew into an art form of their own.
Rosa Ramalho

Rosa Ramalho (1888–1977) learned pottery as a girl, stopped when she married, and returned to it as a widow in her late sixties. Her fantastical figures, devils, beasts with human faces and strange musicians, were noticed by artists and collectors in the 1950s. She is now seen as one of Portugal's great folk artists.
How a rooster is made

steps: Clay shaped by hand or mould
Dried, then fired in a kiln

deep.x: Every workshop has its own touches: the curve of the tail, the pattern of hearts, the colours of the flowers. Sizes range from tiny charms to roosters taller than a child. Many families have passed the craft down through several generations.
City of crafts
In 2017 Barcelos joined UNESCO's Creative Cities Network for crafts and folk art. Its pottery museum holds thousands of pieces, from everyday pots to figurado.

x: Look for the maker's name or mark under the base
Hand-painted pieces differ slightly from each other
Imported copies are usually lighter and more uniform

deep.x: Behind the souvenir rooster is a living craft of potters who shape a whole imaginary world in clay.

cards.text:
O colorido galo de barro é a lembrança mais conhecida de Portugal, mas vem de uma verdadeira tradição artesanal. Barcelos, no Minho, faz louça há séculos com o barro do vale do Cávado.

Além dos galos, os seus oleiros modelam mundos inteiros em barro, o chamado figurado: músicos, diabos, animais e cenas da aldeia, muitas vezes cheios de humor e fantasia.

cards.title: Saudade

steps: A memória fica doce e triste

deep.x: The word comes from the Latin solitas, "solitude", probably influenced by saudar, "to greet". Medieval forms such as soidade appear in the songs of the Galician-Portuguese troubadours.
A king's essay

In the 15th century, King Duarte gave saudade a chapter in his book of advice, the Leal Conselheiro. He described it as sorrow at being apart from someone loved, which can mix with pleasure in remembering them.
Saudade as a national idea

In the early 20th century, the poet Teixeira de Pascoaes led saudosismo, a movement that made saudade the key to Portuguese identity, mixing memory of a great past with hope for the future. Critics saw it as romantic nationalism, and later writers questioned whether one feeling can define a people.
Is it really untranslatable?

deep.w: Saudade cannot be expressed in any other language
deep.r: Every language can describe it in a phrase, and close cousins exist, like Galician morriña and Welsh hiraeth; what is special is how central the word is in Portuguese

deep.x: Brazil even has a Day of Saudade, on 30 January.
Saudade is the presence of an absence: a longing that hurts and comforts at the same time.

cards.text:
A saudade é a falta que se sente de alguém ou de algo ausente: uma pessoa, um lugar, um tempo, até algo que talvez nunca volte. Pode ser triste e doce ao mesmo tempo.

Os portugueses dizem muitas vezes que é intraduzível e veem-na como parte do caráter nacional. Atravessa o fado, a poesia e a fala do dia a dia: "tenho saudades tuas" diz-se em inglês "I miss you".

quiz.q: O que é a consoada?
options: O jantar da véspera de Natal
quiz.explain: Come-se na noite de 24 de dezembro.

quiz.q: Que Carnaval entrou na lista da UNESCO em 2019?
quiz.explain: Os seus caretos mascarados vestem fatos de franjas de lã coloridas.

quiz.q: O que se come num magusto?
quiz.explain: Faz-se por volta do São Martinho, a 11 de novembro.

quiz.q: De quem é a festa de 29 de junho que fecha os Santos Populares?
quiz.explain: Como era pescador, é muito querido nas terras do litoral.

lessons.title: O desporto em Portugal
lessons.summary: Lendas do futebol, hóquei em patins campeão do mundo, ondas gigantes, heróis da maratona, ciclismo e vela.

cards.title: Os três grandes do futebol

deep.x: The national league started in 1934–35 and became the First Division in 1938. Benfica has the most titles, followed by Porto and then Sporting. Their rivalry shapes every season: the Lisbon derby between Benfica and Sporting, and "O Clássico" between Benfica and Porto.
In Europe

Benfica won the European Cup in 1961 and 1962 and reached several more finals. Sporting won the Cup Winners' Cup in 1964. Porto won the European Cup in 1987, the UEFA Cup in 2003, the Champions League in 2004 under José Mourinho and the Europa League in 2011.
More than football

All three are multi-sport clubs, with teams in roller hockey, futsal, handball, basketball, volleyball and athletics. Sporting's academy produced both of Portugal's modern Ballon d'Or winners, Luís Figo and Cristiano Ronaldo.
A popular legend says coach Béla Guttmann, leaving Benfica in 1962 after a pay dispute, put a curse on the club's European hopes. Benfica has since lost eight European finals.
Portuguese football has been led by three clubs for almost a century, and their rivalry is part of national life.

cards.text:
O futebol é o desporto mais popular em Portugal. Três clubes, o Benfica, o FC Porto e o Sporting, ganharam quase todos os campeonatos desde que a liga começou, nos anos 30.

Só dois outros clubes foram alguma vez campeões: o Belenenses em 1946 e o Boavista em 2001. Cada um dos três grandes tem milhões de adeptos em Portugal e no estrangeiro.

cards.title: Eusébio

deep.x: Eusébio grew up in a poor district of Lourenço Marques, today's Maputo, then a Portuguese colony. He played for a local club linked to Sporting, but in 1960 he joined Benfica after a famous tug-of-war between the two Lisbon rivals.

Portugal's first World Cup, in England, made him a global star. Against North Korea in the quarter-final, Portugal were 3–0 down after 25 minutes; Eusébio scored four goals and Portugal won 5–3. They lost the semi-final to the hosts and beat the Soviet Union for third place.
Goals everywhere

x: Top scorer of the Portuguese league seven times
First winner of the European Golden Shoe, in 1968, and again in 1973
Over 470 goals in official matches for Benfica

deep.x: He died in January 2014. A year later his remains were moved to the National Pantheon in Lisbon, an honour given to very few sportspeople. A statue stands outside Benfica's Estádio da Luz.
Eusébio's four goals against North Korea in 1966 remain the most famous comeback in Portuguese football.

cards.text:
Eusébio da Silva Ferreira, nascido em Moçambique em 1942, tornou-se um dos maiores avançados da história ao serviço do Benfica e de Portugal.

Alcunhado Pantera Negra, ganhou a Bola de Ouro em 1965 e foi o melhor marcador do Mundial de 1966, em que Portugal ficou em terceiro lugar.

cards.title: Cristiano Ronaldo

deep.x: Ronaldo left Madeira at 12 to join Sporting's academy in Lisbon. At 18 he moved to Manchester United, where he won three Premier League titles and his first Champions League. At Real Madrid, from 2009 to 2018, he became the club's all-time top scorer with about 450 goals.
Records

x: First player to score at five men's World Cups, from 2006 to 2022
All-time top scorer in the Champions League
First man to reach 200 international caps, in 2023

deep.x: How he stayed at the top

Ronaldo is known for an intense routine of training, diet and recovery. It helped him reinvent his game with age: from a fast winger who dribbled past defenders to a central striker who scores with very few touches.
His name was reportedly chosen in honour of US president Ronald Reagan, whom his father admired.
Ronaldo's career is a story of talent multiplied by work, lasting more than two decades at the top.

cards.text:
Cristiano Ronaldo, nascido no Funchal, na Madeira, em 1985, é um dos futebolistas mais bem-sucedidos de sempre. Ganhou cinco Bolas de Ouro e cinco Ligas dos Campeões.

É o melhor marcador e o jogador com mais internacionalizações do futebol masculino de seleções, e foi capitão de Portugal nos seus primeiros troféus.

cards.title: Finalmente, troféus

events.l: Final do Euro perdida em casa

deep.x: Portugal reached semi-finals in 1966, 1984, 2000 and 2006, and lost the Euro 2004 final at home in Lisbon to Greece. Euro 2016 started badly too: three draws in the group, and a place in the knockouts only as one of the best third-placed teams.
The 2016 final

At the Stade de France, Ronaldo was injured early and left the pitch in tears. Fernando Santos's team held firm, and in the 109th minute the substitute Éder scored with a low shot from outside the area. Ronaldo spent extra time urging on his team-mates from the touchline.
The Nations League

UEFA created the Nations League in 2018 to replace many friendlies with competitive matches. Portugal hosted the first finals in 2019 and beat the Netherlands 1–0 in Porto, with a goal by Gonçalo Guedes. In June 2025, under Roberto Martínez, they beat Germany and then Spain, drawing 2–2 in the final and winning 5–3 on penalties.
Portugal's women's team has risen too: it played its first World Cup in 2023 and drew 0–0 with the reigning champions, the USA.
After many near misses, Portugal became a team that knows how to win finals.

cards.text:
Durante décadas, a seleção nacional jogou futebol bonito mas não ganhou nada. Isso mudou no Euro 2016, em França, quando Portugal venceu os anfitriões por 1–0 na final.

Juntou-lhe a primeira Liga das Nações da UEFA em 2019, em casa, no Porto, e voltou a ganhá-la em 2025, ao bater a Espanha nos penáltis em Munique.

cards.title: Hóquei em patins

deep.x: Teams have four outfield players and a goalkeeper on a rink about 40 m by 20 m, enclosed by a low barrier. The ball is hard and fast, so goalkeepers wear heavy pads. Fouls can bring a blue card, which sends a player off for a short time, as well as direct free hits and penalties.
A golden age

Portugal won its first world title in 1947, in Lisbon, and dominated the following years, winning almost every championship until the early 1960s. Matches were broadcast on radio and drew huge crowds, and for decades roller hockey was second only to football in popularity.
Clubs and towns

Benfica, Porto and Sporting all have strong teams, but the sport is also a passion in smaller towns such as Barcelos, Oliveira de Azeméis and Valongo. Portuguese clubs have won Europe's top club competition many times.

deep.w: Roller hockey is the same as inline hockey
deep.r: Inline hockey uses inline skates and a puck; roller hockey uses quad skates and a ball

deep.x: Roller hockey is one of the few sports where Portugal has long been among the very best in the world.

cards.text:
O hóquei em patins joga-se com patins de quatro rodas, um stick e uma bola dura. Portugal é uma das grandes potências da modalidade.

A seleção masculina já foi campeã do mundo mais de 15 vezes, tendo como principais rivais a Espanha, a Argentina e a Itália.

cards.title: As ondas gigantes da Nazaré

steps: Ondas sobem na Praia do Norte

deep.x: Nazaré was known for its fishing boats and its fisherwomen in seven skirts until 2011, when the Hawaiian surfer Garrett McNamara rode a wave of about 24 m there. The images went round the world, and the town became a pilgrimage site for big-wave surfers.
Records

Measuring a moving wave is hard: judges study photos and video to estimate the height from trough to crest. The Brazilian Maya Gabeira holds the women's record and the German Sebastian Steudtner the overall record, both set at Nazaré in 2020.
How tow-in works

Waves this big move too fast to paddle into. A partner on a jet-ski tows the surfer onto the wave, then races back to pull them out of the impact zone. Spotters on the cliff, rescue teams and inflatable vests are essential.
Surfing beyond Nazaré

x: Peniche's Supertubos hosts a World Surf League Championship Tour event
Ericeira became Europe's first World Surfing Reserve in 2011
Frederico Morais was the first Portuguese surfer to qualify for the Championship Tour, in 2017

deep.x: The best place to watch is the red lighthouse at the Fort of São Miguel Arcanjo, on the cliff right above the waves.
Nazaré turned a fishing town's dangerous winter sea into a world stage for big-wave surfing.

cards.text:
No inverno, a Praia do Norte, na Nazaré, produz algumas das maiores ondas surfáveis do planeta. Um canhão submarino concentra a energia das tempestades do Atlântico.

Surfistas rebocados por motas de água já lá surfaram ondas com mais de 25 metros. Toda a costa portuguesa, de Peniche à Ericeira, é um destino de surf.

cards.title: Heróis da maratona

deep.x: Carlos Lopes, born in 1947 near Viseu, was a track and cross-country runner long before he was a marathoner. He won 10,000 m silver at the 1976 Olympics and the World Cross Country Championships in 1976, 1983 and 1984.
Los Angeles 1984

Lopes broke away in the final kilometres and won in 2 hours 9 minutes 21 seconds, an Olympic record that stood for 24 years. In Rotterdam in 1985 he ran 2:07:12, the first marathon under 2 hours 8 minutes.
Rosa Mota

Rosa Mota, from Porto, won the first women's marathon at a European Championship, in Athens in 1982. She went on to win three European titles, the 1987 world title and Olympic bronze in 1984 before her gold in 1988, and won the Boston Marathon three times.
Porto's domed pavilion in the Crystal Palace gardens carries her name, and the city's road races now draw thousands of amateur runners.
Lopes was reportedly knocked down by a car while training in Lisbon about two weeks before the 1984 Games, but escaped with minor injuries.
Lopes and Mota proved that a small country could produce the world's best distance runners.

cards.text:
A primeira medalha de ouro olímpica de Portugal veio da maratona: Carlos Lopes venceu em Los Angeles, em 1984, aos 37 anos.

Quatro anos depois, Rosa Mota ganhou a maratona feminina em Seul e tornou-se a primeira campeã olímpica portuguesa. Juntos, fizeram do atletismo de fundo uma paixão nacional.

cards.title: Campeões olímpicos

deep.x: Fernanda Ribeiro, from Penafiel, was world champion at 10,000 m in 1995. In Atlanta she followed China's Wang Junxia until the final lap, then overtook her to win in an Olympic record time. She added a bronze in Sydney in 2000.
Jumping for gold

The triple jump is a hop, a step and a jump from one run-up. Nelson Évora, born in Côte d'Ivoire to Cape Verdean parents and raised in Portugal, won in Beijing in 2008. Pedro Pichardo, born in Cuba and Portuguese since 2017, won in Tokyo in 2021 with 17.98 m, then took silver in Paris.
Gold on the track

In Paris in 2024 Iúri Leitão and Rui Oliveira won the madison, a 50 km relay race in the velodrome in which partners take turns, handing over with a hand-sling. Leitão also took silver in the omnium, becoming the first Portuguese to win two medals at one Games.
Portugal first competed at the Olympics in 1912 but had to wait 72 years for its first gold.
Six Olympic golds, five of them in athletics, show where Portugal's sporting strength lies beyond football.

cards.text:
Depois dos ouros na maratona, Fernanda Ribeiro ganhou os 10 000 m em Atlanta, em 1996, com uma última volta feroz.

Nelson Évora e Pedro Pichardo venceram depois o triplo salto e, em Paris 2024, Iúri Leitão e Rui Oliveira conquistaram o ouro no ciclismo de pista. Ao todo, Portugal soma seis ouros olímpicos.

cards.title: A Volta a Portugal

items: Cerca de dez dias no verão

deep.x: The first Volta, in 1927, ran on roads that were mostly unpaved, and riders often had to fix their own bikes. It is one of the oldest national stage races still running, older than Spain's Vuelta.
The climbs

The race is often decided in the mountains. The steep ascent of Senhora da Graça, near Mondim de Basto, and the long climb to Torre in the Serra da Estrela, almost 2,000 m up, are legendary. Summer heat makes them harder still.
Portuguese riders abroad

Agostinho began racing late, after military service in Africa, and won the famous stage to Alpe d'Huez in 1979. He died in 1984 after a crash during the Tour of the Algarve and remains a national idol.
A race for the people

x: Villages decorate their streets as the race passes
Fans gather for hours on the climbs to see the riders for seconds
Live TV brings the landscapes of the interior into homes across the country

deep.x: The record for Volta wins is four, shared by the Portuguese Marco Chagas and the Spaniard David Blanco.
The Volta keeps cycling close to the people, rolling through towns and villages every summer.

cards.text:
A Volta a Portugal, disputada pela primeira vez em 1927, é a grande prova por etapas do ciclismo nacional. Todos os verões atravessa o país durante cerca de dez dias, com multidões a ladear as subidas de montanha.

Os ciclistas portugueses também brilharam lá fora, de Joaquim Agostinho na Volta a França ao campeão do mundo Rui Costa e a João Almeida.

cards.title: A vela e o mar

deep.x: In London in 1948 the brothers Duarte and Fernando Bello won silver in the two-person Swallow class, Portugal's first Olympic sailing medal. In Atlanta in 1996 Hugo Rocha and Nuno Barreto took bronze in the 470 dinghy.
Big events

x: Cascais hosted a round of the America's Cup World Series in 2011
Lisbon was a stopover of the Volvo Ocean Race in 2012 and 2018
The Tall Ships Races have visited Lisbon several times, filling the Tagus with sails

deep.x: The Sagres

The navy's training ship, the NRP Sagres, a three-masted barque with red crosses on its sails, is a floating symbol of Portugal. Built in Germany in 1937, it has sailed for Portugal since 1962 and has gone around the world several times.
Learning to sail

Many coastal towns and river clubs run sailing schools for children, usually starting in the small Optimist dinghy. The windsurfer João Rodrigues competed at seven Olympic Games in a row, from 1992 to 2016.
The red cross on the Sagres' sails is the Cross of the Order of Christ, the same emblem carried by the caravels of the Discoveries.
Portugal's seafaring past lives on in its sailing clubs, regattas and wind-sport beaches.

cards.text:
Com uma longa costa atlântica e um passado marítimo, Portugal tem uma forte tradição de vela. Velejadores portugueses ganharam a prata olímpica em 1948 e o bronze em 1996.

Lisboa e Cascais acolhem regularmente grandes regatas, e a nortada constante do verão faz da costa um destino de eleição para o windsurf e o kitesurf.

quiz.explain: Lopes ganhou a maratona de Los Angeles em 1984, aos 37 anos.
